item.title: Comfy Sunday Spaces v37: OAI/Anthropic Revenues, Neocloud volatility and Trading Philosophy
item.description: Flood and Kyle reprice AI growth after OpenAI and Anthropic revenue claims disappoint expectations. They argue AI financing helped set the marginal price of money, then discuss cash, Bitcoin, and crash prep. Semiconductor multiples and prediction-market valuations look rich unless cash flows justify ownership.
item.content:encoded:
thinkingusd · Flood · 2026-10-18 · 106 min · 原语言 EN

Flood and Kyle reprice AI growth after OpenAI and Anthropic revenue claims disappoint expectations. They argue AI financing helped set the marginal price of money, then discuss cash, Bitcoin, and crash prep. Semiconductor multiples and prediction-market valuations look rich unless cash flows justify ownership.

TL;DR

  • Lower revenue expectations are testing an AI trade priced for exceptional growth. Flood contrasts OpenAI’s rumored $70 billion annualized run rate with its subsequently stated $50 billion, while Anthropic’s leaked roughly $16.8 billion Q3 revenue leaves questions around $100 billion ARR expectations. These remain unaudited claims, but the repricing already hit Nebius, CoreWeave and IREN, reportedly down 30–50% over two weeks: extraordinary technology still faces the “laws of financial gravity.”
  • Kyle’s central macro claim is that AI’s demand for financing is setting the marginal price of money. The 10-year Treasury reached roughly 5.3%, yet yields subsequently fell alongside AI stocks despite hot CPI and PPI releases. His mechanism: less anticipated AI borrowing frees capital elsewhere; a genuine AI rebound could push yields back toward their highs. Developers who believe they are “building God” will keep borrowing until financing costs constrain them.
  • An Anthropic IPO could succeed while draining capital from existing AI holdings. Kyle expects roughly $5 trillion of equity supply over the next year across major offerings and subsequent unlocks, competing for finite risk capital. Circle’s post-IPO surge illustrates his mechanism: investors seeking “the pure AI play” may sell infrastructure proxies to buy the labs themselves, regardless of whether those proxies’ businesses deteriorate.
  • Flood’s defensive position is primarily cash, with a willingness to reverse when the thesis changes. He reports roughly 70% cash versus a usual 80% net-long posture without a strong thesis, retaining smaller Bitcoin and Hyperliquid positions. Flood says he has not seen Bitcoin outperform strongly through material equity drawdowns; Kyle adds that he has never seen it stay flat, much less rise, during one. Renewed equity conviction or inflationary support for AI could change Flood’s view. “I’m gonna wait for the next pitch.”
  • Crash preparation means accessible capital and rehearsed decisions before prices dislocate. Kyle separates buying forced-liquidation rebounds from accumulating durable holdings, while Flood warns that resting bids 10–20% below market still liquidated leveraged traders when altcoins fell 60–70%. Flood’s illustrative shopping level is HYPE at $40, where he would begin buying incrementally. Their framing: “markets are pop quizzes.”
  • Cheap semiconductor multiples may reflect peak earnings rather than overlooked value. Flood describes memory producers earning extraordinary margins while end-user AI economics remain expensive; the market may correctly anticipate that upstream profits will normalize. His valuation test is deliberately uncomfortable: “is every human on Earth gonna spend three thousand dollars a year on AI?” The broader discipline is distinguishing cash flows that justify ownership from stories that merely attract another buyer.
  • Higher rates could eventually strengthen the debasement case rather than undermine it. Kyle follows Jeffrey Gundlach’s framework: sufficiently high sovereign debt can turn attractive Treasury yields into a warning about fiscal sustainability, potentially weakening the dollar and supporting gold, Bitcoin and property. AI distress could also invite inflationary intervention framed as strategic competition with China, which he considers “extremely constructive for Bitcoin and debasement trades.”
  • Prediction-market growth does not settle either valuation or legal durability. Flood calls Polymarket’s $20 billion valuation excessive, including at $10 billion, and prefers ordinary exchange multiples; Kyle pushes back that regulatory uncertainty makes a confident valuation difficult. Kyle sees gambling businesses as relevant comparables. Flood argues crypto needs protections “codified into law” before a possible political reversal in 2028.

Digest

1. Private AI labs create public-market information risk

  • Flood’s opening frustration is informational: enormous public-market exposure rests on two private companies whose revenue, spending and balance sheets outsiders cannot inspect. Even some investors lack information rights. Someone who learns that lab revenue is slowing could make informed trades in public beneficiaries before everyone else. His complaint is “a tremendous amount of asymmetric information,” rather than an accusation that either company falsified its numbers.
  • Flood floats a forcing function for companies raising outside capital at this scale: tens of billions in revenue and hundreds of billions raised might justify public ownership and disclosure. He also suggests allowing annual reporting to reduce short-term pressure. Kyle’s disagreement is explicit: “completely unbothered.” A trillion-dollar furniture manufacturer, he argues, should retain the autonomy to remain private.
  • Kyle’s concern instead follows the technology’s externalities: the labs monetize knowledge contributed across the public web while their products can affect everyone. He cites Anthropic’s proposed donation of up to 20% of its shares to Trump Accounts as an attempt to distribute economic upside without voting rights. Separately, Flood describes cryptography fears, reported hacking, and REA, a reverse-engineering tool he says can use AI to break down compiled programs. Those are Flood’s examples of externalities and potential harms.

2. Annualized run rates leave major questions about revenue and margins

  • Flood stresses that the figures under discussion are rumors and unaudited disclosures. OpenAI’s whispered $70 billion ARR became a company-stated $50 billion. Annualization itself deserves scrutiny: $1 million earned on one day can become a $365 million annualized figure without establishing that the next year will produce that revenue. Markets initially shrugged off the revision before AI names weakened.
  • Anthropic’s investor-meeting leak put Q3 revenue around $16.8 billion, or roughly $17 billion, against earlier discussion of $100 billion ARR. Flood’s possible reconciliation is approximately $25 billion revenue in Q4, supporting that annualized rate. That would require another roughly 50% sequential increase, similar to Q2–Q3, but the earlier period included “token maxing.” He also distinguishes rising costs for heavy API use from falling prices per token.
  • Flood gives the bull case its strongest form: these might be “the best businesses on Earth,” with profitability obscured by pre-training. He cites inference as only 37% of data-center usage; shifting 90–100% toward inference could produce a massive gross-margin business. The question is whether those economics survive when the spending that maintains frontier performance stops.
  • The bear case is commoditization: without continued pre-training, users might migrate to free open-source models or subsidized competitors. Flood’s analogy is economy air travel, where passengers largely want the same destination and acceptable delivery rather than a particular carrier. If the “end product, the end state” dominates purchasing decisions, frontier intelligence may struggle to retain premium economics for ordinary tasks.

3. Neoclouds sit inside an amplified spending chain

  • Kyle separates outside customer demand from transactions within the AI complex. His estimate is roughly $250 billion in annualized spending by customers outside that complex, amplified into trillions as companies purchase from one another. Nvidia hardware enters CoreWeave facilities, networking comes from Broadcom, and servers consume AMD or Intel CPUs and memory. That “amplification factor” makes many securities sensitive to the same underlying demand.
  • Kyle thinks some earlier growth reflected Chinese model distillation that the labs knowingly tolerated because it generated revenue and helped fundraising. In his explanation, blocking those customers subsequently flattens growth and unsettles downstream suppliers. This is his interpretation of the revenue trajectory; the discussion supplies no internal company evidence establishing it.
  • Flood reports Nebius, CoreWeave and IREN falling roughly 30–50% over two weeks, even with the broader market still up around 15% year to date. Kyle points to widening credit-default-swap protection on CoreWeave and Oracle as investors identify potential casualties. His concern is what happens if the labs are “only like seventy percent as good as we thought they were.”
  • Neither claims a trading edge in those names. Financing structures, construction delays, political obstruction and contractual responsibility require specialist knowledge they say they lack.

4. AI financing may now govern the cost of money

  • Kyle recalls the 10-year Treasury reaching approximately 5.3%, alongside a rate hike, while equities initially resisted the pressure. Then hot CPI and PPI arrived, yet Treasury yields fell as AI sold off. His provocative reading is that inflation is not currently the dominant marginal variable; anticipated borrowing for AI is driving the market’s pricing of capital.
  • The relevant distinction, in Kyle’s framework, is whether next year requires $500 billion or $1 trillion of AI borrowing. Strong demand makes financing expensive and competes with other borrowers. An AI slowdown reduces that competition, making capital more available to governments and businesses outside the sector. Falling yields can therefore accompany deteriorating expectations for AI rather than better inflation news.
  • His conditional test is concrete: if the sell-off proves to have been a fund liquidation and AI stocks recover, Treasury yields should probably return toward their highs. If AI continues unwinding, financing should keep getting cheaper, potentially reaching the two-year Treasury and expectations for no further hikes. Neither outcome is presented as certain.
  • Kyle believes developers who think they are “building God” will borrow every available dollar to accelerate, whether motivated by AGI or competition with China. Higher financing costs finally impose a ceiling. That is why he says fixed-income investors are currently “in the driver’s seat”: their pricing of default risk and funding determines what the rest of the trade can sustain.

5. An AI IPO can rally while starving its proxies

  • Anthropic’s S-1 remains the major unresolved catalyst. Flood allows that it could reveal “the greatest company on earth” and squeeze bears. Kyle is more suspicious of delays: Polymarket’s probability of an IPO that year fell from roughly 94% in early September to around 70%, with only about 50% for completion by November’s end. He also cites limited information-sharing and renewed safety concerns.
  • Flood discusses a rumored $1.5 trillion valuation versus an earlier $2 trillion ambition, with approximately $200 billion sought. Kyle combines potential Anthropic and OpenAI issuance, subsequent unlocks and SpaceX supply into roughly $5 trillion of equity looking for buyers over the next year. These are prospective supply estimates, not completed offerings, but they underpin his caution toward risk assets.
  • Kyle’s best analogy is Circle: investors wanted a pure stablecoin business rather than partial exposure through Coinbase or PayPal, and the shares surged within three weeks. Portfolio allocation to a theme could overwhelm valuation. He expects similar demand for “the pure AI play,” potentially making Anthropic perform very well while investors sell correlated infrastructure holdings to fund purchases.
  • Flood also watches existing companies issuing equity to finance capital expenditure. Management is choosing to sell ownership rather than borrow more; that counterparty decision deserves attention. He does not treat it as an automatic instruction to liquidate, but as another reason to reconsider sizing while the market works out AI’s eventual economics.

6. Flood’s cash position follows his equity thesis

  • Flood reports approximately 70% cash, retaining Hyperliquid and Bitcoin in substantially smaller quantities. The context matters: without a strong thesis, he typically runs around 80% net long because of his underlying enthusiasm for crypto. He also says Bitcoin sold during the reduction delivered almost a $2,000 gain per coin. Cash is his current allocation decision: “I’m gonna wait for the next pitch.”
  • Flood says that in nearly a decade and a half in crypto, he has not seen Bitcoin trade exceptionally strongly while equities sold off materially—10%, 15% or 20%. Kyle adds that he has never seen Bitcoin remain flat, much less rise, through such a decline. Its continuous trading and liquidity often make the drawdown larger. Betting on an exceptional decoupling is therefore insufficient reason for Flood to retain his usual exposure.
  • A bullish change in equities would likely bring rapid crypto re-entry; highly inflationary preferential financing for AI could also change Flood’s view. Their defensive posture includes low-double-digit-percentage shorts, rather than a huge crash bet. Flood considers a 10% market decline the following week exceptionally unlikely, and Kyle emphasizes that their equity framework operates over approximately six months.

7. A thesis needs an invalidation and a matching time horizon

  • Flood wants an identifiable price level, fact or state change that proves a thesis wrong. Otherwise, recognition can arrive after substantial losses. His own sensitivity to rising rates comes from complacency in 2022, when his portfolio was “eviscerated.” He also warns that social feeds reinforce positioning: liking one bearish CoreWeave post caused his feed to fill with similar arguments.
  • Winning frequently is a different objective from making money. Flood cites fellow trader Basics TNZ reporting roughly a 30% win rate despite substantial profits; sizing the strongest opportunities can dominate the result. His requirement is emotional flexibility: losses become more damaging when a trader cannot admit error or change exposure.
  • Kyle’s timeframe warning is that a six-month thesis can coexist with painful daily reversals, including 3–4% rallies and 10% up weeks. Flood’s example is Hyperliquid: buying in single digits and selling around $30 worked, but approaching $100 required enduring major tests, including Jelly Jelly and competition from Lighter. A short-term trading rule can interrupt a longer-term investment thesis.
  • Flood and Kyle manage separate books and can disagree, so one visible wallet does not represent every position or view. Flood also rejects taking trades to defend an online reputation. “You get paid for being fluid and responding to state changes,” rather than letting social pressure choose the trade.

8. Crash preparation starts with capital that can actually move

  • Kyle’s first rule is to avoid being incapacitated on the day. Capital behind a seven- or 30-day staking unlock cannot fund an immediate opportunity. Then distinguish two strategies: buying a forced-deleveraging overshoot, perhaps in a leveraged ETF such as SOXL, or accumulating assets intended for holding over one to three years. Those require different selection and exit decisions.
  • His rehearsal scenario runs from a terrible Anthropic S-1 through missed spending commitments, distressed neoclouds, trouble at Oracle and Nvidia’s backstops creating contagion. The purpose is to pre-decide a response while calm. He explicitly says such a dramatic sequence “almost certainly won’t happen”; preparation is useful without making the scenario a forecast.
  • Flood’s cautionary example is traders leaving bids 10–20% below market before altcoins fell 60–70%, liquidating even 2×-leveraged positions. Cross-margin accounts can also fail during a momentary 90% drop. Venue outages and congested chains matter independently of insolvency: capital on the wrong platform can leave a trader unable to act during the crucial hour.
  • Flood’s illustrative plan is HYPE at $40: begin buying a specified dollar amount every minute and welcome lower prices, because he considers levels underneath attractive. A shopping list does not require unattended limit orders. “Markets are pop quizzes”: preparation can determine whether a rare dislocation produces double-digit gains or losses, rather than leaving the trader frozen at the screen.

9. Falling markets force stories back toward cash flows

  • Kyle describes ownership fatigue after a stock falls in 18 of 20 weeks: “Why the fuck do I own this?” His framework is that markets oscillate between cash flows and stories. Prices can climb as high as a persuasive future allows, but durable bottoms require an ownership case based on being paid back within a reasonable period and with acceptable risk.
  • Zoom supplies his historical example: the story that offices, classrooms and business communication would permanently migrate to one remote platform supported extraordinary expectations. “The stories work until they don’t.” In a prolonged decline, investors may prefer businesses whose valuations need less storytelling, even at the cost of sacrificing upside.
  • Flood’s tweet cited companies moving from $50 million to $10 billion valuations within months. He says that implies $9.95 billion of value creation by a relatively small team. Kyle calls it effective storytelling. Flood adds that a VC’s claimed 1× downside protection depends on an acquisition actually occurring. Their preferred reading includes Buffett and Howard Marks for longer-term allocation judgment, rather than weekly market calls.

10. Debt stress could reverse the usual response to higher rates

  • Asked whether the 1970s oil shock, rate increases and gold’s more-than-tenfold rise offer a useful parallel, Kyle says historical comparisons will likely fail here. He follows Jeffrey Gundlach’s framework: normally higher Treasury yields attract investors away from non-yielding gold, but sufficiently large government debt can make higher rates look like a sustainability warning instead of an attractive opportunity.
  • If debt-service costs consume an alarming share of tax revenue, Kyle thinks the result is “probably dollar down” and probably supportive of gold, Bitcoin and even property. Separately, worsening AI distress could invite extraordinary support framed around beating China. He sees that potential intervention as constructive for debasement trades, which helps explain why he is less anxious about crypto’s longer-term position than about equities.

11. Prediction-market valuations depend on law as well as growth

  • Flood considers Kalshi reasonable but is publicly bearish Polymarket at $20 billion and even $10 billion. His comparison is an exchange: he cites Nasdaq around 8× and suggests 5–10× as reasonable multiples, rather than 20×, 40× or 100×. The sector may grow, but implementation and competition leave him broadly neutral to somewhat bearish on current companies at their valuations.
  • Kyle’s pushback is “I don’t know that it’s way overvalued,” because legal uncertainty makes the business itself difficult to handicap: the operators might not have a business in two years. Robinhood’s prediction revenue attracted growth enthusiasm, but he sees much activity substituting for exchanges or sports betting. MGM and DraftKings therefore look like relevant comparables, implying lower valuations than private markets currently assign.
  • On the midterms, Flood distinguishes ordinary political gridlock, which markets often welcome, from crypto’s need for affirmative legal protection. Without legislation such as the CLARITY Act, a Democratic presidency in 2028 could reverse today’s tolerance; prediction markets are particularly exposed. Flood’s intuition is that Democrats probably win the midterms and will then be favored for 2028, rather than that either outcome is certain.

12. Cheap chip earnings and expensive AI services can coexist

  • Asked whether institutions are simply chasing stories like retail traders, Flood says valuation depends on where one looks. He describes SK Hynix and Micron producing extraordinary earnings, citing roughly 90% net margins and enough profit to repurchase their shares at current prices in about three years. Earlier, Kyle noted some chip names trading at approximately 3–4× earnings. Those securities can look strikingly cheap.
  • The catch is overearning: circular spending can make supplier profits unusually strong, while low multiples signal that the market doubts their durability. Flood says the market may be right to price chip companies cheaply. Conversely, assessing Google, Microsoft, Amazon or Meta solely on AI revenue against AI spending would make those activities look extremely expensive; their other businesses soften the consolidated picture.
  • Flood does expect AI revenue to rise as people learn productive uses over time. His unresolved test is the scale of spending required to justify expectations: “is every human on Earth gonna spend three thousand dollars a year on AI?” Otherwise, as he puts it, “a lot of the math isn’t mathing.”

来源：X Space

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/comfy-sunday-spaces-v37-oai-anthropic-revenues-ne

item.title: 新的创业机会，正在 Claude Code 和 Codex 周围长出来｜对谈 Treg
item.description: Trig以单Key按量收费、无月费，聚合Agent数据与工具；上线约三周收入已是Super Design好几倍，付费集中在Go-to-market。Codex插件几乎无宣传却为Super Design带来大量低流失用户；Trig中间层能否持续创造价值仍待验证。
item.content:encoded:
十字路口Crossing · Koji、Jason Zhou、石天鑫 · 2026-10-18 · 51 min · 原语言 ZH

Trig以单Key按量收费、无月费，聚合Agent数据与工具；上线约三周收入已是Super Design好几倍，付费集中在Go-to-market。Codex插件几乎无宣传却为Super Design带来大量低流失用户；Trig中间层能否持续创造价值仍待验证。

TL;DR

  • Trig（Jason Zhou 与石天鑫的创业项目）把自己定位成“面向数据和工具的 OpenRouter”——给 Agent 用的数据与 API 市场，用一个 Key 即可访问想要的数据或工具，纯按量付费、没有月费。 发布约三周后，收入已是前一个产品 Super Design 的“好几倍”；付费最集中的场景是 Go-to-market：找 B2B 客户、SEO/AEO 数据，以及整合上百种 AIGC 相关模型的 UGC 视频链路。
  • 九个多月、三四次转型的过程，反复在回答模型变强后应用如何创造独立价值的问题。 Super Design 开源后几个月获得六千多个 GitHub Star，完全自然增长；Jason 认为开源是 AI 产品的重要营销工具。不过创业后他们没有继续走开源路线：当时没看到 IDE 插件的好商业化路径，也希望做网页版，让更多人能直接使用。Gemini 3 等模型的前端能力提升，加上 Claude Code/Codex 的通用 Agent 和 Skill 生态发展，也让 Jason 重新思考设计 Agent 的增益在哪里。
  • 二到六月是 AI employee 创业的“魔幻时间”，但 Jason 团队做 Crewlet 后发现，未来六到十二个月“零人公司”不是可行场景。 Jason 认为 Posia 最聪明之处，是把从零到一的业务搭建做得极其顺滑；但进入真实业务后，要交付结果、帮助公司赚钱就难得多。Crewlet 的经验也让他们看到，营销没有万能方案：渠道效果会变化，判断哪些关键词未来会增长，仍很需要人的判断。
  • 另一条结论是围绕 Claude Code 和 Codex 生态做产品——Jason 用 Facebook 之于 Zynga、eBay 之于 PayPal 作类比。 一个几乎没有宣传的 Codex 插件改变了 Super Design 的增长曲线，带来大量用户，且这部分用户流失率更低。石天鑫观察到插件市场早期按字母顺序排序，于是把名字改成“01 Super Design”，短暂排到第一位。
  • Trig 的定位是中立聚合数据与工具，并用 Agent 反馈形成数据飞轮。 Jason 认为每个场景都有许多各有所长的供应商，许多供应商缺少直接触达终端用户的方式；Trig“更像一个 Costco”。石天鑫提出，产品的用户也包括使用者的 Agent：可以让 Agent 评价 API 返回的数据是否有用，积累各端点的有用度和性价比信息，供后续用户选择。
  • 生态红利也体现在模型套餐与工具需求上：石天鑫说，Codex 和 Claude Code 用户可以用 200 美元的编程套餐，获得价值 6000 到 7000 美元的 API Token 使用量。Apify、DataForSEO、Exa、Firecrawl 等服务也被嘉宾举作生态机会的例子；石天鑫说 Exa 应该已到 C 轮，Jason 则表示 Firecrawl 的用量如今大约一半来自开发者、一半来自终端用户。Koji 介绍的多 Agent 管理工具 Orca 已有 8 万 GitHub Star，Jason 说有些用户同时跑 50 到 100 个 Session。
  • 工具栈和职业判断都在随模型变化。 Jason 从 Claude Code 重度用户转用 Codex，主要因为 Astra 模型强；他常同时开 5 到 10 个 Session，并把 Trig 与 Super Design 的 Loop 搬到 Grok Bot。模型按场景各有用途：Kimi 曾用于设计，MiniMax Hailuo 用于生成视频，石天鑫偏爱 DeepSeek 4.1 Flash，也认为速度很快的 Jeff 模型可用于路由和数据过滤。谈到职业选择，石天鑫认为程序员已很难写得过 AI，自己因此加入创业团队；Jason 则认为跨领域能力可能更容易发挥出来。

Digest

1. 九个月、三四次转型，都在回答同一个问题

  • Koji 的开场定调：Jason 团队表面上似乎一直在找方向，背后其实和这个时代很多 AI 应用创业者一样，在回答同一个问题——“当基础模型越来越强，AI 应用公司究竟应该如何创造独立、差异化的价值”。
  • 路线图：设计 Agent Super Design → 全自动增长 Agent Crewlet → 现在的 Trig，“面向数据和工具的 OpenRouter”，给 Agent 用的数据和 API 市场——用 Claude Code、Codex 或搭建 Agent 时，不必逐家购买订阅，一个 Key 就可以访问想要的数据或工具。
  • 背景速览：Jason 此前在澳洲创业公司 Relevance AI 负责产品和 AI 团队，三年多前就在做全自动销售、SDR；石天鑫在苹果中国短暂实习后，陆续在阿里、字节待了十年。Jason 去年年底出来创业。

2. Super Design：六千多个 Star 的开源项目，模型前端能力提升后开始重新思考增益

  • 起点是一个可能只是周末项目的产品：Jason 做 YouTube 频道时发现 UI 设计相关视频流量很大，于是做了 Cursor 插件——说一句需求，就能出三四版设计供选择；开源后几个月获得六千多个 GitHub Star，而且完全是自然增长。他由此总结：“开源是 AI 产品赛道里非常重要的营销工具。”
  • 辞职创业后，他们没有继续走开源路线，也从 IDE 插件转做网页版：当时没看到插件形态较好的商业化路径，也觉得插件要求用户先使用 Cursor、Claude Code 或 Codex，网页版可能更方便更多人开始使用。Jason 后来感叹，接下来一年大家却都涌入了 Codex 和 Claude Code。
  • Koji 把 Super Design 的变化概括为“模型吞噬应用”的故事。Jason 说很难预测：Gemini 3 出来后，各大厂商开始提升前端能力；与此同时，Claude Code 和 Codex 作为通用 Agent，配合热门前端设计 Skill，也能做出不错的效果。他们因此思考，模型越来越强时，自己的增益到底在哪里。

3. 二到六月的魔幻时间：Posia 把从零到一做得极致顺滑

  • Jason 对那段时间的描述值得留存：“今年二月到六月是一段很魔幻的时间。”他看到大量优秀创业者转向 AI employee 赛道，因为大家用了 OpenClaw，觉得“the future is coming”。几个月后停下的原因很朴素：这件事比想象的难。
  • 触发点是 Posia：Jason 说它当时的 ARR 可能只有十几万美元，但产品体验让他非常震撼——“上一次有那种感觉，应该是第一次用 Cursor”。只凭邮箱，Posia 就能搜索 Jason 的背景、生成两三个创业想法，并很快搭好落地页。Koji 亲测后被推荐做 AI 播客后台，很快付费；两天后 Jason 问他充了多少钱，Koji 说又充了几百美元、开了 God Mode。后来 Koji 没继续跟进：“没有帮我赚到钱，只帮我花了钱。”
  • Jason 做同类产品后才看懂 Posia 的优势：它听起来像是要让 AI 掌管公司所有链路，但实际交付做得最好的，是帮用户搭建业务——把从零到一做得非常顺滑。进入真实业务后，要交付结果、帮助用户赚钱就难得多。Jason 还指出，Posia 的产品形态看起来不太可靠；对于已有业务的公司，也不能接入内部系统、产品分析和广告系统。

4. Crewlet 的教训：交付增长结果需要人的判断

  • Crewlet 的设想是给已有业务的公司做全自动增长团队：SEO、社交媒体和内容营销、广告自动调整预算、Cold Email 找客户。产品发布后，虽然还没准备好，他们仍放了付费墙让用户预购；有不少用户愿意付费，但真正要交付结果时，团队发现很难。
  • Jason 的核心诊断是：“营销没有一个万能方案。”真正有效的渠道，往往要经过大量尝试，发现某种方式做的人不多、又适合自己，再不断加码；但当大家都做时，这个渠道可能又没那么有效。因此，在不断变化的过程中很需要人的判断。
  • 承载论点的例子：Agent 做 SEO 的工作流，是找相关关键词，比较流量和竞争，再选择关键词。但他们发现，大多数关键词早就被抢得差不多了；真正有机会的，可能是当前流量不高、但判断未来一个月或三个月会变热的词——这很难让 Agent 完全独立完成。

5. 停下开发两个月，换来两条确定性

  • Crewlet 做了一个多月后，Jason 反思是不是步子迈得太大：他们还没验证“零人公司”是否是未来，就因为试过 OpenClaw 和 Posia，而假设它一定会到来、模型六个月内一定足够强。于是团队停下产品开发，尝试用 AI 运营仍有自然流量的 Super Design：若能验证全自动运营和增长，就能了解方法；若不行，也能排除这条路。
  • 两个月的结论之一：客服确实可以全部自动化，修复 Bug 也可以自动化；但增长相关的应用场景少，因为需要人介入测试的地方太多。Jason 因而判断，未来六到十二个月，“零人公司”不是可行场景，更需要解决人和 Agent 大量协作的问题。第二个结论是：“一定要围绕 Claude Code 和 Codex 生态做产品。”
  • Jason 认为这段“不做产品”的时间收益很大：“那两个月帮我梳理并确信了对未来的一些判断。”否则他们可能还在迭代 Crewlet，纠结 Skill 是否做得不够好、Prompt 是否调得不太行。创业时不确定性很多，有相对确定的判断会好很多。

6. 一个插件改变增长曲线，外加一次字母排序的小聪明

  • 增长实验试了不少，Jason 觉得都没什么用；真正改变增长曲线的，是石天鑫上线的 Codex 插件。没有宣传，大量用户涌入；后来他们发现，这部分用户的流失率也更低。
  • 石天鑫还原细节：Codex 刚发布 Work 和插件市场时，还没有太多有意思的插件。他们几乎没做什么，只把原来的 CLI 和 Skill 发布进去，就赶上 ChatGPT 和 Codex 的大用户群。更妙的是，他观察到市场早期按字母顺序排序，于是把名字从 Super Design 改成“01 Super Design”，排到了第一位。几天后排序规则就改了，但这个起步带来了一些流量。他的启发是：早期工具和市场都值得尝试，因为不知道哪次尝试会带来流量。
  • 由此生长出 Trig：复盘 Crewlet 的资产时，他们认为各家的 Harness 差别不大，真正可迁移的是工具和数据那一层——Agent 做真实 Go-to-market 工作需要大量专业数据和工具。团队本来就为 Crewlet 做了一层中转服务，于是把它单独拿出来发布。上线约三周后，收入已是 Super Design 的好几倍；具体数字不便分享。Trig 完全按用量收费，没有月费。

7. Trig 是 Agent 的 Costco：聚合各有所长的供应商

  • 付费最多的场景集中在 Go-to-market：海外找 B2B 客户，原来需要购买 Apollo、RocketReach 等不同供应商的服务；每家只覆盖一部分数据，又按月收费，用户往往只能选一家。聚合之后，用户可以按场景和行业挑合适的端点。SEO、AEO 排名和 AI 可见度数据源，以及社交媒体、UGC、生图生视频的端点也在其中；Jason 说，他们整合了基本上所有能找到的相关数据源。
  • 对“工具为何愿意被整合、收入可能减少”的回答是：很多垂直领域供应商没有很好的方式接触终端用户。Jason 举 Clay 为例：它背后的数据大部分不是 Clay 自己的，而是来自一批数据提供商；Clay 整合数据后再转卖给用户，而这些数据提供商原本就按 API 用量收费。
  • Jason 的定位是：“我们站在一个中立的位置”，让用户以较高性价比获得满意的数据，“更像一个 Costco”。关键在于每个场景都有几十个不同供应商，各有优势；找人、SEO 和 AEO 等领域都不是一家头部供应商就能提供最好的方案。

8. 护城河拷问：模型会不会跳过这一层

  • Koji 提出两层疑问：Claude Code 和 Codex 不接 Trig 也能做一些事情，未来会不会不需要中间层？即使聚合模式成立，价值为什么会留在 Trig，而不是由最强的数据供应商直接对接模型公司——Trig 会不会只是对接尚未完成时的阶段性价值？
  • Jason 回应，业务工作需要的数据是实时的，不是 Claude Code 开箱即用就知道的；浏览器自动化也拿不到所有数据。比如找人，不是 Google 一搜就能搜到；做社交媒体时，也有平台会限制数据获取。
  • 石天鑫补充了一个方向性观察：他的朋友选择 Kimi，是因为 Kimi 接入了万得股票交易数据。他认为，各家 Agent Harness 可能会因为接入的数据有独特性而吸引用户。Trig 则提供中立市场，让各家 Harness 都能用同一批工具；用户从 Claude Code 切换到 Codex 时，之前积累的工具调用和数据也可以留在这里。

9. 产品的用户也包括 Agent：大众点评式的数据飞轮

  • 石天鑫的关键认知是：“现在很多产品真正的用户已经不只是人了，还有这个人的 Agent。”他们有机制随机挑选用户，让用户的 Agent 给反馈；简单的 Bug 直接修复，有意思的功能请求则收集后考虑是否加入。
  • 他还提出一种数据飞轮设想：Trig 有时可以让 Agent 用户评价 API 调用，比如返回的数据有没有用、哪个字段起了作用；这些反馈可以透明沉淀下来，形成各领域不同 API 端点在有用度和性价比上的评分图表。图表结合客观数据与 Agent 主观反馈，帮助后续用户的 Agent 选择工具：需要精确性时选更贵、更好的端点；需要覆盖面和低价时选性价比高的工具。
  • 他把这归为 AI 应用创业团队可以采取的方案：“既然我们没法训练自己的模型，总要让一些数据反哺自己的产品。”

10. 生态里正在长出来的公司，和 200 美元换六七千美元 Token 使用量的红利

  • Jason 点名的增长样本：Apify（长尾爬虫 API 市场）和 DataForSEO 存在很久，今年突然有大量增长；设计领域的 Paper 增长也很快。Jason 认为 Paper 的做法与 Trig 转型后的方向相似：提供画布，让用户在 Codex 原有工作流里对比、手动微调设计。石天鑫补充：据他了解，为 Agent 做搜索的 Exa 应该已到 C 轮；Composio、Firecrawl 等提供网页抓取、OAuth 授权和工具的公司最近也获得了较大增长。Jason 说，这类公司的用量现在大约一半来自开发者，一半来自终端用户；后者可能是不懂编程的白领，只知道接入 Firecrawl 后 Claude Code 就能更高效地抓网页。
  • Koji 补充的生态案例：Eagle 是用 Codex、Claude Code 做 Computer Use 时效率很高的浏览器；ChatCut 的 Codex 剪视频插件提供可见的编辑器中间状态。没有中间状态，修改视频可能只能重新生成成片，每次要等十分钟或二十分钟，还会消耗很多 Token；有了中间状态，Agent 可以操作音轨、片段等接口，节省时间。Jason 说自己用 Hyperframe 时仍更愿意给 Agent 反馈，让它来修改。
  • 还有黑客松冠军 Vibe Island：利用 MacBook 灵动岛管理多线程任务，Koji 说它后来在 X 上发布后卖了很多份，Jason 和石天鑫都付费了。Koji 也介绍了晶晶做的 Orca——ADE（Agent 的 IDE），可以同时管理多个编程 Agent，并在 Codex 配额用完时把任务转到 Claude Code。Koji 说它已有 8 万 GitHub Star；Jason 透露，有些用户可能同时跑 50 到 100 个 Session，新的 Agent 交互方式可能是一个机会。
  • 石天鑫点出这个生态的经济结构：小创业公司向模型公司买 Token 再卖给用户，压力会很大；而 Codex、Claude Code 用户“可以用 200 美元的编程套餐，获得价值 6000 到 7000 美元的 API Token 使用量”。用户和小创业公司都要想清楚怎么利用这个机会。Jason 用 Facebook 之于 Zynga、eBay 之于 PayPal 作类比；他还说，今年以来各工种使用的工具似乎都转向 Claude Code 和 Codex，这是一次较大的平台迁移。

11. Loop Engineering 的务实版：创新 Loop 不了，运营可以

  • Koji 提到当时流行一两周的“Loop Engineering”。石天鑫认为，把创业分成创新和运营两部分，创新显然不是 Loop 能完成的；否则说“帮我造一个创业公司”，它就能造出来。运营侧则有许多踏实可做的事。他提到自己喜欢《系统之美》，书里讲如何搭建系统，让它稳定运行、健壮生存；开环和闭环反馈都是其中的讲究，他认为 Loop 是 Agent 领域的有效工具。
  • 承载论点的例子：四人创业团队要应对黑客攻击；只要有邀请新用户、赠送 Credits 等激励机制，就可能不断遭到攻击。长期监控系统、寻找风险行为并堵住小漏洞的 Loop，可以节省团队精力。
  • 方法论是 Loop 不要一开始就建得太复杂，短小精炼的 Loop 反而更有用：一个只监控数据库、寻找安全风险，另一个只整理代码。每次做的事情小一些，不容易出错；十几个小 Loop 配合起来，也可以形成更健壮的系统，例如一个 Loop 提交了 Bug，线上监控 Loop 还能找到问题并提示。

12. 工具栈实况：Astra 让 Jason 转用 Codex，Grok Bot 承接 Loop

  • 最近两三个月最大的变化是并行度：Fable 等模型发布后，Jason 基本同时开五到十个 Session，因为它们自己完成任务的质量已经很高。其次是从纯本地转向 Grok Bot 带来的云端加本地混合体验，可以随时交换 Context。Jason 说 Trig 和 Super Design 的 Loop 都搬到了 Grok Bot；他认为 Grok Bot 并没有太多创新，但云端沙盒体验很顺滑。他还说 Grok Bot 收购 Cursor 很合理，因为 Cursor 的优势之一是为每个编程任务提供沙盒，本地很难同时测试五六个不同环境。
  • 阵营选择上有真实分歧：Jason 几个月前还是很难迁移出来的 Claude Code 重度用户，Astra 模型出来后转用 Codex，主要因为模型很强。他们常用 Hyperframe 做宣传视频；Jason 说有一次把参考视频交给模型，它一次性、一比一地复刻出来，还能从原视频截图、裁剪素材，再放进新视频。石天鑫则倾向于两个都用，因为他认为两者没有绝对领先优势；他会把一些任务同时交给两个模型，再挑更好的版本。
  • 国产模型按场景分工：Kimi 曾被尝试作为 Super Design 的主模型，Jason 认为它设计能力强；MiniMax 接入的是 Hailuo 视频生成模型，质量高、价格也不错。石天鑫喜欢 DeepSeek 4.1 Flash，认为效率高、速度快；他考虑过把 Super Design 的第一层 Agent 换成 DeepSeek，但目前 Claude 在大量场景下可能更稳定，因此还没有在生产环境切换。
  • 对 Jeff 模型，Jason 认为它速度足够快，能实现一些原本不太可能的场景。石天鑫当天刚开始接触，提出两个用例：端点请求需要快速路由时，等待几百毫秒也可能浪费时间；以及对两三千条召回结果进行清洗。若有一个“像 System 1 直觉一样”的模型逐条比较，他认为可能做出很好的召回引擎，比其他 LLM 快很多、质量也不差。

13. 把才华埋葬在昨天之后：十字路口上的职业与信念

  • DeepSeek 研究员的文章《我不得不把我的才华埋葬在昨天》引出石天鑫的自白：他前十年主要做程序员和前端开发，擅长 React；从去年开始，他意识到这项技能的意义变小，除非做到世界前几百名。后来他加入 Super Design，开始和 Jason 团队做有意思的事。他认为程序员已经很难写得过 AI，人生十字路口上的选择可能带来很大变化；Jason 补充，跨领域能力未来可能更容易发挥出来。他自己是一个不喜欢调 Pixel、喜欢从产品经理角度看问题、也会写前端代码的设计师。
  • 两人都坦承想过放弃。Jason 说做 Crewlet 时不确定的事情太多，每天都在想下一步；他的判断准则是，思考当前方向上有没有什么事能真正改变处境，想不到可能就要换方向。他做 YouTube 频道，过小康生活相对容易，所以也有过想放弃的时候。石天鑫则说自己经历过崩溃时刻：事情长期没有增长、不断受打击，甚至醒来发现 Credits 被盗刷、一下损失 4000 美元，会觉得天塌了。团队一直寻找其他方向和机会，让他们能朝有希望的地方努力；他也认为，如果确定一件事要失败，不如让它快速失败，再尝试新东西。
  • 收尾于 Koji 转述的问题：相信 AGI 会到来、认为它由模型进化带来，却仍然创业的人存在吗？Jason 说模型是 AGI 到来的必要条件，但路径有很多；团队沉浸在最新技术前沿，才能对未来六到十二个月的机会有较好直觉。石天鑫认为，即使 AGI 到来，做性价比高的事情仍然有用：即便有一个万能模型，也需要工具和数据；如果它花 1000 美元 Token 才得到的数据，Trig 能用 100 美元提供，它可能就会选择 Trig。

来源：Podcast

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/shizilukou-2026-10-18-claude-code

item.title: market update
item.description: 金老师认为，行业认知与数据调用加密支撑 AI 和半导体长期需求，股价下跌不代表需求见顶。利率波动经信用、FX 和股票流动性传导；利率压力减轻，但信用利差未修复，伊朗扰动油价仍可能重启压力。企业后训练需求和短租算力价格是周期验证信号；2027 年的卡、电、钱已有准备，2028 年及中国供应链出海风险仍不确定。
item.content:encoded:
Shanghao Jin · beefcube (execute/commies)、tmomoh、Wil、Xiaoxiao Geng、书米亚光环、Doggy Su、Ryan · 2026-10-18 · 91 min · 原语言 ZH

金老师认为，行业认知与数据调用加密支撑 AI 和半导体长期需求，股价下跌不代表需求见顶。利率波动经信用、FX 和股票流动性传导；利率压力减轻，但信用利差未修复，伊朗扰动油价仍可能重启压力。企业后训练需求和短租算力价格是周期验证信号；2027 年的卡、电、钱已有准备，2028 年及中国供应链出海风险仍不确定。

TL;DR

  • 金老师把可持续的 Alpha 放在行业认知上，维持对 AI 与半导体的长期看多。 他两周前提示流动性风险，却没建议清仓，因为看见风险不等于能准确交易风险；在其量化经验里，散户频率下的单一量价因子很难提供稳定优势。过去5—8年，sell put 赚的主要仍是“市场涨的钱”；偶尔躲中两次下跌，也可能只是幸存者偏差。
  • 他的核心判断是数据与半导体的调用正在加密，市场尚未准备好让半导体成为最大的产业。 从互联网把纸面数据搬进电脑，到移动互联网增加访问，再到 AI 高频调用，需求扩张的逻辑并不只取决于 chatbot 收入。半导体在他眼里是算力够不够的“零和一”：若真相信2027—2028年会砍单，TSMC、ASML及其上下游都无法独善其身。
  • 他把本轮下跌归因于利率波动引发的流动性传导，反对用股价下跌倒推需求见顶。 路径是利率波动扩大，冲击 credit、主权 credit 与 FX，再由 credit 传到 CDS 和股票；他认为利率端的对冲及强平压力已经减轻。未来3—6个月关税效应下降也支持利率回落，但信用利差尚未修复，伊朗继续扰动油价仍可能让“上游的水源”重新打开。
  • 他不认为 CoreWeave 会被 CDS 单独挤成另一家雷曼。 按其口述，该公司 PP&E 约460亿、净负债约300亿、现金约80—100亿，operating cash flow 为正且大概覆盖利息；约一半融资还有 GPU 抵押或云厂支持。他承认 CDS 上升会损害融资、形成负反馈，但判断较差结果更可能是减少投入，缺口仍可被其他买家吸收。
  • 企业 post-training 是他认为市场尚未充分定价的需求来源。 通用模型需要吸收企业数据与 knowhow，才能从聪明的“博士生”变成能工作的员工，而且需要持续训练。他给出的微软相关需求量级是年初约20亿、目前约200亿；同时，短租和周末算力租金没有出现他所要求的过剩信号，因此不接受仅凭 Anthropic 增速放缓就宣布算力过剩。
  • 他对 Labs 的长期价值判断，正从模型能力转向高价值场景中的数据积累与直接经营。 用户一边付费、一边贡献后训反馈，Labs 因而可能自己进入搜索、量化交易等业务。他已经卖掉 Google：原先担心的是搜索广告收入，现在连搜索效果的垄断也开始怀疑，“Search 赛道，你最后的效果也不确定是谁好谁坏”。
  • 金老师预计 Anthropic 的 IPO 可能破发，同时强调模型公司与半导体可以走出不同结果。 他认为35倍或40倍 PS 不是交易成败的关键，降价25%所显示的融资迫切，以及 allocation 中长期资金与 hedge fund 的比例更重要。“不管它什么价格上市，它都有可能会破发”，并不等于他认定整个算力周期结束。
  • 他对2027年卡、电、钱的准备较有信心，对2028年和中国供应链出海则保留不确定性。 按其了解，2027年不会因电力问题普遍砍项目，2028年“不知道”；中国光通信企业面临的潜在阻力，则可能来自境外建厂受限。中际旭创即使按提问者所说只有11—12倍明年 forward PE，产业能力与“供货的可靠性”仍须分别判断。

Digest

1. 看见风险不等于拥有交易风险的 Alpha

  • 金老师两周前提醒流动性可能变差，却没有建议清仓，因为当时上下行风险相对对称。其出发点是：“你不要瞎操作”，看见一个风险指标，并不代表能把它稳定交易成收益。
  • 按其量化经验，implied vol、恐慌指数、盘口等单因子，在散户可执行的频率下很难提供可靠 Alpha；毫秒级交易、多因子组合，或掌握 prime broker、做市商仓位，则可能有优势。
  • 他称过去5—8年唯一较有效的简单策略是 sell put，赚的仍是“市场涨的钱”；他认为 sell call 不赚钱，即使持续卖出，过段时间回头看也是这样。一年躲中两次下跌，就觉得自己厉害，往往混入了幸存者偏差。
  • 基本面判断可能要两三年甚至五年兑现，不能拿来要求每天的价格配合。他用德州“开了底牌”比喻行业认知：若进场是为了吃 fundamental Alpha，“那你就拿着不要动”。

2. AI 周期的底层变化是数据调用密度上升

  • 金老师把三轮周期串起来：互联网将纸面资料搬进电脑并连接起来；移动互联网让人更频繁访问积累的数据；AI 则让数据与半导体的接触变得更加紧密、频繁。
  • 因而，他关注的不只是“AI 能干多少活”，而是数据、半导体再到能源的持续扩张。即使每个 token 的价格下降，也不能直接推出半导体需求下降。
  • 他认为现在处于“end or beginning”：最初靠想象冲进去，等真实需求和资金出现，反而迎来质疑。他承认此前也怀疑过 AI 想象空间，如今判断 CSP 对企业需求的补充会更快。

3. 下跌的起点在利率与信用，需求质疑在后

  • 金老师强调，三四周前利率上涨本身不是最危险的信号，利率 vol 同时上升、超过临界点才是。油价与利率挂钩后，战争带来的油价波动被传导到庞大的利率衍生品市场。
  • 冲击蔓延至企业信用、主权信用及 FX；南美货币在股票下跌前已经很弱。他判断，两三周前欧洲债券市场的恐慌，甚至比当下股票市场更严重。
  • 看空需求的叙事，相当于认定云厂下单不负责、TSMC及更上游订单都不可靠，进而给2027—2028年砍单定价。他不同意：“因和果不要倒置”——先跌、再质疑需求，与需求先坏掉是两回事。

4. 利率端开始止血，信用市场尚未恢复

  • 金老师认为，这次 CPI 比上个月更难看，利率反应却较温和，原因主要是他所称的 convexity hedge 压力减轻。非农之后，十月加息已经“off the table”，并非几位联储委员讲话才改变预期。
  • 他把 swaption 的集中平仓比作股票 gamma squeeze，并判断这轮挤压接近结束。利率更有均值回归特征，因此在当前高波动位置，“现在去卖 swaption，我肯定会去卖”。
  • 其判断是“上游的水源已经断掉了”，但并不等于流动性宽裕：部分信用利差，以及法国、意大利、西班牙国债 spread 仍高。除非伊朗进一步制造冲击，他暂未看到源头继续恶化。

5. 对冲基金可能在流动性薄弱处猎杀杠杆仓位

  • 金老师用“hunting elephant”形容短线交易：离中期选举约两周，市场又要为融资需求准备现金，财报前买家也不愿部署资金，资金便可能选择边缘市场施压。
  • 周四、周五盘后密集出现的新闻，让他怀疑有人试图挤出已知的大额杠杆仓位。他明确把这称为自己的观察和判断，认为 AI 链条最脆弱的 neocloud 环节容易成为目标。
  • 他与前高盛同事讨论的真正担忧，是 CDS 上升会抬高融资成本，再反过来制造危机。这个负反馈值得重视；但他认为当下做空短期较安全，拉长时间则风险很大，不能据此认定整个行业已经变质。

6. 2008年的关键是底层资产已经坏掉

  • 金老师回顾，2008年 mortgage 的 delinquency rate 已经上升，损失先吃 equity、再吃 mezzanine，而 CDO 又由 mezzanine tranche 合成。他提到，CDO和super senior最终都可能亏约40%，底层现金流的问题是真实存在的。
  • 雷曼还持有大量难以定价、彼此关联的衍生品，政府又放任杠杆集中平仓。他认为若当时提供流动性，局面不会发展成那样；当前 CoreWeave 既没有同等规模与关联度，也缺少相同的底层资产恶化，不能直接套用2008年。

7. CoreWeave 的信用判断要落到资产与融资结构上

  • 谈到 CoreWeave，金老师称其约一半融资为 senior unsecured，spread 已涨到约15%；另一半是 secured、collateralized，或有云厂支持的融资，不能把所有债务视为同一种风险。
  • 他口述 PP&E 约460亿，场地主要租赁，资产大部分是芯片、连接、电源等生产设备；净负债约300亿，现金约80—100亿。他让听众对照 H100、A100 的二手价格，判断这些资产实际能回收多少。
  • 公司状态并不好，但他强调 operating cash flow 为正，“大概能覆盖利息”，并判断资产可以抵债。这与底层抵押物已出现现金流损失的 CDO，是其眼中的关键区别。
  • 对于 CDS 能否直接将公司挤成 default，他说“我觉得不可能”。其设想的较差结果是减少投入、转让或打包出售项目；在算力与电力仍紧缺的情况下，他认为其他买家能够吸收相应需求。

8. 半导体押注算力短缺，美国与韩国的仓位条件不同

  • 金老师把半导体归结为“零和一”：认为算力不够就是一，认为已经过剩就是零。真正砍单时，从设计公司到 TSMC、ASML 都会受影响，换到产业链另一端并不能避开同一个需求判断。
  • 他选择“一”，理由是前端订单与更前端需求仍满，并称整体 forward PE 已回到 GPT 发布前水平。同时，他认为美国市场整体杠杆、仓位都不高，个别“大象”高杠杆不等于全市场如此。
  • 对韩国，他仍认为存储紧缺，但不接受 margin 到90%的推演。韩国去杠杆后重建杠杆较快，相比之下，他觉得美国的仓位条件使其风险收益更有吸引力。

9. 三到六个月的利率判断押注关税效应退潮

  • 金老师以十月不加息、十二月可能再加一次为观察框架，认为未来3—6个月关税效应下降较确定。去年十月政府关门可能干扰同比数据，因此他更重视十二月、一月的表现。
  • 他解释，关税的滞后影响可能在今年三四月见顶，之后逐月减弱；对核心通胀的影响“大概零点八”，是很大一块。要继续制造通胀，得新增关税，不能重复计算原来那次提价。
  • 油价同理：维持100与继续涨到150不同，后者取决于伊朗是否持续扰动，他承认不知道、但倾向认为较难。供给型通胀下，加息“不可能多生产一头牛”；他判断近期利率涨得过多，未来有回落空间。

10. 企业后训要把博士生变成能工作的员工

  • 金老师的比喻是，再聪明的博士生，也不能每天拿“一本员工手册，加上四本 skill”反复阅读，就直接替企业工作。模型需要吸收企业自己的数据与 knowhow，后训需求因此不能只从 chatbot 增长推算。
  • 提问者问 post-training 是否指 CSP 根据客户资料挑选垂类来训练，金老师先回答“不是，不是”；随后举例说明企业可以借助 Microsoft 或 Amazon，在自己的数据上训练模型。他给出的微软相关需求量级是年初约20亿、目前约200亿，并建议关注微软、Amazon 如何谈 corporate AI 需求。
  • 企业可能更敢把资料交给服务多年的 Microsoft；他形容：“你比较敢交给 Microsoft，它服务你的 SaaS 多年，要偷你的数据早就偷了。”云厂的部署与客户场景，也是其竞争优势。

11. 高价值场景的反馈，比通用能力排名更能积累壁垒

  • 金老师认为，用户一边付钱使用、一边贡献后训反馈，模型与数据形成双向循环。这使 coding 的先发优势难追，也让他判断中国模型厂中被低估的是字节，不是 DeepSeek：重要的是已经占据高价值场景。
  • 他用自己的 BN 下单需求举例：多台服务器算完后，要在同一毫秒抵达同一 AWS 地点。早期 Anthropic 完全不懂这些调度 knowhow，如今简单描述就能做得“七七八八”，他自评效果强过有经验团队做一星期。
  • 他也称，自己给较小模型标注网络小说资料、再训练后，写小说效果比通用模型更好。后训不是一次性工程，企业数据会新增、流程会改变；他同时承认，后训完成后采用小模型，推理需求也可能低于预期。

12. 卖掉 Google，源于对搜索垄断的判断改变

  • 金老师原先认为，AI 不读广告，会损害 Google 搜索收入，但搜索能力本身仍是永远的垄断。现在他改了看法：“Search 赛道，你最后的效果也不确定是谁好谁坏。”
  • 按其比较，去年其他搜索加总约为 Google 的0.5%，年初 Anthropic 使用的搜索约到20%；他猜测如今即使到70%—80%也“不奇怪”。他提到 Brave，并用香港地铁出口查询举例：OpenAI 有时比 Google Maps 更好用。
  • 他的进一步推演是，Labs 积累足够反馈后可能亲自进入高价值业务，包括量化交易。即使 Jump、Tower、Jane Street，若面对懂筛因子又拥有更多算力的 Labs，也未必有优势；他说的是未来可能性，并非这些 Labs 已经全面入场。

13. Anthropic 增速放缓，尚不足以证明算力过剩

  • 提问者提出具体反驳：Anthropic MoM 若降到约5%，平推年增约80%—90%，而未来两年算力规划翻倍，在 CSP 后训收入尚未披露前，市场的负面 equity story 是否有基本面依据。
  • 金老师认为 Anthropic 降价不好，并拆出两种影响：per-token 价格可能受 OpenAI 价格战压制，开源模型影响则“还没有那么严重”；供给不足、部署进度也可能限制收入，不能直接等同于算力过剩。
  • 他要求看租金验证：on-demand 短租至少应接近长约价格，才像供应过剩；目前短租仍紧，周末租金也没下降。他据此判断训练需求仍强，“那些说不要这么快训练模型的人”，基本上还在私下训练。

14. Anthropic 的 IPO 风险在融资需求和买方结构

  • 金老师说“不管它什么价格上市，它都有可能会破发”。半导体只需判断算力够不够，前端模型公司却各有场景、竞争与商业化问题；微软、Amazon 的企业入口强，并不意味着独立 Labs 一样容易获利。
  • 对降价能否改善交易的追问，他认为35倍与40倍 PS 没本质区别，情绪可以把估值推到50倍、100倍，也能砸到20倍。降价首先传递的是“很想融”、很 desperate。
  • 他更重视 allocation：优质长期投资人抢不到额度、发行人不愿分给 hedge fund 的 IPO，通常更好。降价后很难挑买家；他以当年的 Facebook 为例，融资覆盖广泛、卖到 retail，不保证初期交易表现。

15. 中国模型限制可能推动更多自建算力

  • 对中国模型可能限制使用或出口，金老师判断现有开源内容“关回去也没有用”，眼前、乃至往后半年都不会因此受影响。但他认为未来政策发生的概率较大，理由是决策体系中反对“领先技术需要管制”并不容易。
  • 在需求端，他认为这反而可能令微软等企业从“备用一个自己的模型”，转向必须有自己的模型。既然企业后训是大头，就不能假设 DeepSeek 永远继续开源，自有模型与算力仍要建设。

16. 中国光通信的潜在阻力在境外供货可靠性

  • 金老师称听到的政策风险，是中国企业去泰国等地建厂，可能被视为对美国妥协，因而遭遇境内阻力。他保留了不确定性，但担心这会影响中际旭创等公司继续担任美国 CSP 一线供应商。
  • 即使最终仍由中国工厂生产，也可能转成经其他供应商分包，因为买家不仅看产能，还看“供货的可靠性”。他认为明年封装测试需求仍强、各环节缺货，短期业绩未必立即受损，但境外新增产能可能由别人建设。
  • 提问者以中际旭创明年约11—12倍 forward PE、所谓 FCC 65%规定及东山精密港股 IPO 追问。金老师承认不擅长 A 股估值映射，也未给出东山对标 AAOI 的明确结论；他更确认中际的封装能力，同时强调中国方面的政策风险。

17. 2027年的卡、电、钱有准备，2028年仍未知

  • 对美国电力审批、BE 装机上限会否导致砍项目，金老师回答：“明年不会，后年不知道。”站在2026年看2027年，他了解到主要 CSP 已有电力储备与替代方案。
  • 他把准备拆成三件事：卡从哪里来大致确定；缺电时用已有未联网储备、燃气涡轮或 BE 等方案；融资和 operating cash flow 也已纳入计划，准备发行的债务约4,200亿。
  • 他反对直接套用2000年互联网泡沫：当时部分公司想投就投、乱买服务器，而当前大公司是在测算需求与资源之后投入。这是他对2027年相对有信心的依据，并非对2028年作保证。

18. 华虹、中芯的改善空间与中国溢价要分别估值

  • 金老师认为华虹、中芯都是不错的公司，但过去有客户要求制造 GPU、CPU，把 DUV“当 EUV 用”，多次曝光压低 margin。他说这家公司最近已不在“遥遥领先”的名单上；对于后续相关方向，两家公司的 margin 可能改善。
  • 他仍坚持晶圆厂最终要看 PB：华虹约三点几倍，GFS 约两倍。提问者以国内“唯二的两个独苗”解释估值，他认可这里包含“中国溢价”，却不认为因此可以忽略其他市场的替代选择。
  • 作为对照，他提出 Intel 的拆分假设：CPU 若按盈利5、20倍估值，对应100，晶圆厂的隐含 PB 就接近零。这是其估值框架，而非对 CPU 盈利已经兑现的陈述。

19. CRWV 的业绩缺口尚未解释，不宜自动升为重仓

  • 对 CRWV 应算彩票还是重要仓位，金老师只回答自己的选择：“肯定不会把它当成一个重要仓位。”他卖掉 Google 后，也没有直接把资金全部转到半导体；相较之下，他愿意给 INTC 较大仓位。
  • CRWV 的问题是，部分资金方按 TSMC 供应链订单推算出很好的业绩，公司却没有报出预期。究竟是有产能没体现，还是产能中途打折，他说“不太清楚”；虽然当前倾向看多，缺口仍未消失。
  • 他提醒，同跌之后，其他基本面更确定的股票可能跌得更多，机会不能只按自身跌幅排序。若这轮是在猎杀杠杆，他认为听到大基金爆仓可能是买盘信号：“一般来说这种砸盘都是砸到有人死掉就结束。”

20. Intel EMIB 的瓶颈要区分封装良率与基板供应

  • 最后一轮，提问者担心 EMIB 的基板与小硅片结构容易变形、影响良率。金老师纠正：“良率很好，没有问题”，他认为问题在供应商的基板良率，后果主要是可供基板不足、限制出货量。
  • 提升这部分良率要靠供应商投入，Intel 作为甲方也须花钱推动；他用 HBM 作类比：“你是甲方，花钱就能提高。”按他听到的消息，目前供货应该 OK，但基板良率提升仍取决于供应商。

来源：X Space

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/market-update-20261018

item.title: Managing $525 Billion by Rethinking Wealth Management | Kurt MacAlpine, Corient
item.description: Corient, now managing about $525B across 15 jurisdictions, applies a professional-services partnership to wealth management, with roughly 3,000 employees on one compensation plan and one P&L. Its roughly 50-deal engine targets founders approaching a $3–5B scale ceiling; the September 2–3, 2025 announcement of acquisitions of Europe’s largest and second-largest UHNW wealth-management businesses advances MacAlpine’s global ambition.
item.content:encoded:
David Senra · David Senra、Kurt MacAlpine · 2026-10-18 · 80 min · 原语言 EN

Corient, now managing about $525B across 15 jurisdictions, applies a professional-services partnership to wealth management, with roughly 3,000 employees on one compensation plan and one P&L. Its roughly 50-deal engine targets founders approaching a $3–5B scale ceiling; the September 2–3, 2025 announcement of acquisitions of Europe’s largest and second-largest UHNW wealth-management businesses advances MacAlpine’s global ambition.

TL;DR

  • Kurt MacAlpine built Corient—now managing about $525B across 15 jurisdictions—by diagnosing wealth management as “built on a fundamentally flawed structure” and rebuilding it as a professional-services partnership. In many advisory businesses, independent-contractor advisers can take clients from colleagues, leaving the client experience tied to the originating adviser rather than the firm. Corient applied a partnership model, drawing on examples such as McKinsey and law firms; MacAlpine calls it “the first true professional services partnership” applied to wealth management.
  • The alignment mechanics are central to Corient’s model: about 3,000 employees on one compensation plan with no exceptions, one P&L with no chargebacks, and a fee-only fiduciary standard. MacAlpine claims Corient is “the largest business in the world that operates under that standard of care,” so any larger firm has the ability to operate at a lower standard. Corient also owns aircraft for clients’ collective use, takes the balance-sheet risk and the risk associated with the monthly management fee, and charges clients based on usage.
  • The M&A engine—about 50 deals—targets entrepreneurs hitting a scale ceiling, not retirees cashing out. MacAlpine’s thesis: a wealth firm can reach $3–5B with a limited service set, but the investments required to reach $50–100B can make the risk-reward trade-off “out of balance.” Joining Corient lets founders become partners and access its services from day one while continuing to grow their businesses. Corient’s median partner is in their mid-40s, versus an industry median adviser probably in their early 60s.
  • The public-market chapter is a conviction case study: CI Financial was the best- or second-best-performing North American financial-services stock in 2021 and the second worst in 2022. MacAlpine used cash flow and leverage to fund the pivot, carrying 3–3.5 turns of debt. The debt was fixed-rate and without covenants, with some debt extending out to 30 years. With about 75% of the float active, including hedge funds and value mutual funds facing redemptions, he bought back shares he called “criminally undervalued” at $12–13: “we were buying and buying and buying and buying.”
  • The take-private highlights a public/private-market disconnect: MacAlpine says private-equity investors would recognize the buyback-and-transformation approach as “the standard blueprint” for operating businesses and extracting value. Mubadala Capital approached him, saying the buyback path would take about nine years and involve execution trade-offs. The deal closed August 12, 2025, with no incremental debt and either deleveraging or an equity infusion tied to it, no cost synergies, and no change of strategic direction.
  • On September 2–3, 2025, Corient announced it was buying the largest and second-largest ultra-high-net-worth wealth-management businesses in Europe. MacAlpine says no truly global UHNW wealth manager exists outside Corient: in his view, multi-jurisdictional banks’ regional P&Ls and compensation structures can make cross-border collaboration an “impossible situation.”
  • The operating philosophy is built around a long horizon: full day-one integration of acquisitions, brand advertising in every market where Corient operates, and a Miami headquarters chosen from a clean slate. MacAlpine wants “the forever business in ultra-high-net-worth wealth management”; he contrasts that with temporary owners thinking in 18–36-month increments and optimizing for an exit. Senra closes with his friend Sam Hinkie’s line: “The person with the longest-term view in the room wins.”

Digest

1. A first-time CEO at 39 takes over a Canadian asset manager and makes a hard right turn

  • MacAlpine’s framing of the business today: partner and CEO of Corient, “the largest multi-family office in the world and the largest non-bank wealth manager serving ultra-high-net-worth clients,” managing about $525B across 15 jurisdictions.
  • The starting point was CI Financial, a Toronto Stock Exchange-listed Canadian asset manager that had been public for about 25 years, earning “several hundred million a year of EBITDA” almost entirely from Canadian mutual funds. MacAlpine said the outlook for mutual funds was tapering relative to areas such as ETFs and alternatives. The board hired him at 39, before he had been a CEO, after he outlined the transformation in the interview: launch a U.S. ultra-high-net-worth wealth business, with the hope of later globalizing it.
  • His philosophy on inertia: “Often times people get comfort when things aren’t changing. That’s when you should be the most uncomfortable... I’m the most nervous when things aren’t changing.” Bill Holland, a previous CEO and chairman, and Ray Chang had built scale in Canadian asset management through acquisitions focused on mutual funds—an earlier disruption of a subscale industry.

2. The diagnosis: a barbell industry built on a flawed structure

  • Three reasons MacAlpine chose UHNW wealth management. First, the tailwinds: “There’s more wealth being created today than ever. That wealth is more concentrated than ever. There’s more complexity tied to that wealth than ever. It’s transitioning generations faster than ever. And it’s more global than ever.”
  • Second, the barbell: large banks that theoretically can do everything but whose governance, bureaucracy, and internal conflicts mean “they give back a lot of the scale benefits that clients should ultimately be benefiting from”—versus small local firms doing exceptional work but facing scale limits on manager access, purchasing power, and services. “In between... there’s a tremendous amount of white space.”
  • Third, the structural flaw: almost all advisory businesses, in his view, are built around advisers who are “independent contractors sharing somebody’s brand, somebody’s technology, and somebody’s office space.” They compete for clients and can take clients from one another within the firm. “Most wealth businesses are built to serve advisers. We wanted to build a wealth business that was built to serve clients.”
  • The three tensions he maps: adviser-to-adviser silos; advisers versus front-office experts (tax, planning, and family-office services can act as cost centers, so the adviser asks whether bringing in an expert will have “a negative impact on me personally”); and compensation that rewards advisers for generating revenue and then hoarding it—“the more that you share, the less that you ultimately earn.” He sees the client as a loser, and the firm itself as another: these businesses become “platforms” rather than companies.

3. The fix: a professional-services partnership, drawing on consulting

  • MacAlpine’s insight came from asking what wealth advisers do: they run “the ultimate human capital business,” requiring EQ and IQ. He points to partnerships in management consulting, law, accounting, and many successful investment and advisory businesses. Wealth managers, he said, had not adopted that structure. “We created the first true professional services partnership and applied it to the wealth management industry.”
  • On ambition and focus, his view is that “human nature guides people towards optionality... you can be fine at a bunch of those things, but it’s very very hard to be world class ultimately at something.” Senra interjects: “I find optionality disgusting, by the way.” Corient’s aspiration since launch has been to be the best in the world at serving UHNW clients globally.

4. What “comprehensive” looks like: embedded tax expertise, trust companies, and aircraft

  • The stack behind the adviser “relationship quarterbacks”: global financial planning (“everything associated with your lifetime”), wealth transfer (“everything that extends beyond your natural life”), 175 people on the investment team split about 70% traditional and 30% alternative investments, and several trust companies, including use of South Dakota in the U.S. Corient also has more than 100 full-time accountants who provide tax advice and implementation and are embedded on wealth-advisory teams, including in trust structuring and investment conversations about harvesting losses.
  • The family-office services include bill pay, outsourced CFO services, customized reporting, concierge lending, complex residential real-estate projects, art management, and aviation. Corient owns aircraft for clients’ collective use, takes the balance-sheet risk of buying the assets and the risk associated with the monthly management fee, and clients pay based on use. Senra frames this as a “Costco shared-economy” model; MacAlpine describes the aircraft arrangement but does not explicitly say it is not a profit center.
  • The logic of bundling: planning, wealth transfer, investments, tax, and trusts can be treated “as a collective problem as opposed to five or six individual decisions,” which MacAlpine says can lead to “meaningfully better outcomes.” But “you can’t do it if you have a structure in place that prevents you from being able to achieve that.”

5. “Conflict-free” defined: fiduciary standard plus less structural friction

  • MacAlpine claims Corient is “the only truly conflict-free business in wealth management,” on two axes. Standard of care: Corient is fee-only and fiduciary, “operating essentially at the highest standard of care.” He claims it is “the largest business in the world that operates under that standard of care. So anyone larger than us has the ability to operate at a lower standard of care.”
  • Business model: about 3,000 people, “one compensation plan” with “no exceptions,” because different compensation can make it “very very hard for us to objectively serve a client.” And one P&L with no chargebacks, since segmented P&Ls and chargebacks “inherently create underlying friction” that can keep experts away from clients.
  • When Senra tests the north star—serving clients better regardless of industry norms—MacAlpine agrees: “Correct. Exactly.” He argues for deep specialization by client type: “the more specialized you are, the more relevant you are, the better advice that you can ultimately give.”

6. Why founders join: the $3–5B inflection point and the Rockefeller parallel

  • The scale pitch to clients: access to capacity-constrained managers, negotiated rates passed through to clients (“whenever we negotiate better rates for our clients, we pass those rates on”), potentially better lending rates, and services that a $5–15B wealth manager would find “virtually impossible” to offer at scale.
  • The pitch to founders: “I don’t think of it as us buying people’s firms. People are coming to be partners at Corient.” His inflection-point thesis: firms can reach $3–5B with a limited set of services, but the investments required to reach $50–100B can make “the risk-reward trade-off” get out of balance. Joining Corient offers access to its existing services while founders continue their entrepreneurial journey. Senra offers Rockefeller’s Standard Oil as a historical parallel—building a “company of founders” by opening the books and exchanging stock—and MacAlpine agrees with the comparison.
  • The demographic consequence is deliberate: the industry’s median adviser is “probably in the early 60s”; Corient’s median partner is in their mid-40s, and its median employee is in their 30s. “We’re not doing M&A to fund retirements. We’re doing M&A to bring on partners who will continue to grow their businesses.”
  • The partnership is also a screening mechanism: “we tend to be someone’s first choice or their last choice... it’s rare that we would come in second.” That self-selection supports the “strategic, cultural, and financial alignment” he says a human-capital business requires.

7. The public market hated it: best stock in 2021, second worst in 2022

  • The volatility, in MacAlpine’s approximate terms: “In 2021, we were the best or second-best-performing financial services stock in North America. In 2022, we were the second worst.” His explanation starts with fairness to the market: “public companies don’t typically love transformation stories,” and CI was using a Canadian mutual-fund business’s cash flow to build a new U.S. UHNW business.
  • The structural amplifier: strategic investors and indexes locked up roughly 25% of the float, leaving about 75% active. He describes hedge funds piling in during 2021 and leaving in 2022, while value-oriented mutual funds faced net redemptions: “every single morning people wake up having to sell your shares to fund redemptions.”
  • On leverage, he carried 3 to 3.5 turns of debt against an asset-manager comparison group where about 2 turns is a rule of thumb. He argues composition mattered more than the amount: the debt was fixed-rate and without covenants, typically with long durations, and some extended out to 30 years. “At no point during the journey did I change my conviction,” though he says he expected the business success and diversification benefits to show up in the share price faster.
  • Senra’s parallels are Bezos, whom he recalls quoting Ben Graham during Amazon’s early stock decline, and his friend Adam, the founder of AppLovin. Senra says he thinks AppLovin’s value fell from about $28B to $3B; he recalls Adam borrowing “another $5 billion or something” to buy back stock while people around him thought it was crazy, and says Adam later described the outcome as worth $50–60B.

8. Buybacks at $12–13 and the public/private-market disconnect

  • Through his tenure, MacAlpine says CI was doing two things: building Corient and reducing the share count because he felt the shares were “criminally undervalued.” He saw forced selling as a buying opportunity: “that creates a tremendous buying opportunity... and we were buying and buying and buying and buying.” They bought many shares at $12 or $13, ultimately taking the company private.
  • The broader point: “If you describe that to a private equity investor, they would say that’s the standard blueprint under which we operate businesses and extract value.” He sees a disconnect between how people assess a business as owner-operators and how they assess its shares in public markets. Investors want diversification “without the time, investments, or capital required to do it,” he argues, but “that’s just not practical.”

9. Mubadala’s approach and a take-private with no synergies or strategic pivot

  • Mubadala Capital approached MacAlpine about two years before the conversation. Its message was that the buyback path would take about nine years and create trade-offs around executing the core strategy. “I agreed with 100% of that.”
  • Terms he emphasizes as evidence of alignment: announced in November 2024 and completed August 12, 2025, with no incremental debt and “deleveraging or an equity infusion” tied to it, no cost synergies, and no change of strategic direction. His verdict on the partner: “the best strategic partner on the planet” with equal ambition. He also says “a Canadian mutual fund company never really belonged in the public markets anyway.”
  • On September 2 or 3, 2025, Corient announced it was buying the largest and the second-largest UHNW wealth-management businesses in Europe. MacAlpine says that would have been an impossible transaction to execute as a public company.

10. The global white space: multi-jurisdictional banks are not global wealth managers

  • MacAlpine’s claim is that “there are no global ultra-high-net-worth wealth managers in the world today” outside Corient, only multi-jurisdictional banks. His reasoning: offices in multiple jurisdictions can still operate as regional P&Ls. In his hypothetical, a billion-dollar family consolidates assets from four jurisdictions in Miami; three regional P&Ls lose assets while one gains. At the adviser level, he says, three people’s pay could go to zero for serving the client while one person’s pay could quadruple—an “impossible situation.”
  • Corient’s answer is the U.S. partnership model globalized: one compensation plan worldwide and one P&L, with clients served across jurisdictions rather than mapped to regional silos. Asked whether he is obsessed with incentives, MacAlpine reframes it: “I’m obsessed with alignment.” He says employees are paid for what they deliver, regardless of whether they joined through a direct hire in Seattle or an acquisition in San Diego.

11. Day-one integration, a crowdsourced name, and advertising for a forever business

  • Integration had three phases: accumulating scale during roughly the first 18 months, beginning the integration journey, and reaching today’s fully integrated state. MacAlpine thought people might prefer the first phase because it involved less change; instead, “people are most comfortable with the current state because they know exactly what they’re getting into.” Full integration means “on day one, you’re on our brand, you’re using our technology, you’re working in our offices... you’re on our comp, you’re on our benefits.” He adds that acquisitions should improve both sides: “I make you better and you make me better. If those aren’t true... it becomes a financial transaction.”
  • The naming story illustrates his integration philosophy. Rather than dictate a brand, he ran focus groups with about 75 participants, had the finalists mocked up under the same branding, and held a live vote at a partner town hall. “On day one, every person who wanted a voice in the process had one”; he says people embrace change better when they see their input reflected.
  • On marketing—prompted by Senra remembering Corient as the sole sponsor across four ad breaks of an interview he thinks was on CNBC’s “Wealth”—MacAlpine says the company advertises in every market where it operates to “short-circuit the discovery process.” He ties the spend to time horizon: “I think this should be the forever business in ultra-high-net-worth wealth management.” He contrasts that with temporary owners thinking in 18–36-month increments and “optimizing for a return and an exit,” rather than building a brand across generations. Senra closes with his friend Sam Hinkie’s line: “The person with the longest-term view in the room wins.”
  • Miami was a clean-slate headquarters choice. MacAlpine launched Corient around April 2020, chose the headquarters at the end of that year, and says he had no historical corporate tie directing him to a location. He cites Miami’s local engagement and welcoming environment, including Francis Suarez’s role as an ambassador for the city. His concern about local talent availability was answered at the time and, he says, has become less of a concern with subsequent migration. He says the choice has worked out beyond his expectations.

来源：YouTube

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/managing-525-billion-by-rethinking-wealth-manage

item.title: 硅谷坐标 x 谷歌DeepMind研究副总裁 Ed H. Chi（纪怀新）：个性化通用助理的未来
item.category: 硅谷坐标 Silicon Valley Vector
item.description: 通用助理仍处早期，权限与可靠性尚无实际订票数据；Ed Chi预计6–12个月后，其与AI Mode Search的界面关系会更清晰。模型能力若普及，Google全栈及低成本token供给或成成本护城河；能力差距收窄则可能让价值更多流向重视黏性与体验的应用。
item.content:encoded:
硅谷坐标 Silicon Valley Vector · Ed H. Chi（纪怀新）、曹卿云 Qingyun Cao · 2026-10-18 · 32 min · 原语言 ZH

通用助理仍处早期，权限与可靠性尚无实际订票数据；Ed Chi预计6–12个月后，其与AI Mode Search的界面关系会更清晰。模型能力若普及，Google全栈及低成本token供给或成成本护城河；能力差距收窄则可能让价值更多流向重视黏性与体验的应用。

TL;DR

  • Ed Chi 判断通用助理仍处“很初期的阶段”，并给出 6–12 个月的时间表：届时通用助理与 AI Mode Search 之间的关系和 interface 会更清楚。权限与 reliability 是卡点——大家会担心把信用卡交给通用助理后，它到处乱买东西；至于它帮人买机票究竟买对还是买错，这类实际结果的数据至今还没有真正出现。他用 Grandma Test 描述通用助理的成熟标尺：“当你的 grandma 指着你的机器人骂它‘你怎么这么笨’，你就知道通用助理的时代真的到了。”
  • 他强调，经济活动最终要看 capability over cost；若模型能力普及，成本控制可能成为最重要的护城河。Google 的优势在于 full stack——从模型、application、hyperscaler、token factory 到芯片与能源控制，并有能力以最低成本提供 token。Ed 也指出，现阶段很多人还没有关注 cost。
  • 关于模型竞争力，他认为 Google 不可能放弃模型开发，理由是用户期待 Google 拥有自己的模型技术。近几个月发布偏小模型是刻意为之——通用助理和个人化应用需要小模型；更大的模型也在开发中。他还提到湾区一些 AGI-pilled tech bros 信奉 software took over the world，因此热衷 ultra-size model；他个人不希望手机应用都跑超大模型，因为计算能耗太高。
  • 他认为，把能力商品化或开源与闭源模型差距的走向说成定论还不成熟。开源模型能追上，其中一个原因是借助他合著的 Chain-of-Thought 论文所述方法研究并复制推理方式；大厂正在设法隐藏推理链，以降低被复制的可能性。Multimodality 等能力目前也还看不出会被商品化。市场并非整体都是泡沫，但不同领域可能各有泡沫；Physical Intelligence 可能有不切实际的预期，很多模型的 visual reasoning 也很糟糕。
  • 若今天创业，他认为模型能力的差距若缩小，value creation 会更多流向 application 和 token factory。Application 端看用户 lock-in、stickiness 与体验；hyperscaler 端则涉及能源用量、芯片设计、memory 与 computation 的关系，以及 on-device 计算的占比——这些仍是 open questions。
  • Memory 是他眼中尚未被充分理解的瓶颈：它不只是存取，也涉及 ranking。Transformer 的 context buffer 目前约一两百万 tokens，在他看来完全不够；从认知角度，memory 也是一种 program。至于 DRAM、NAND、HDD 的供应短缺，他认为 memory 与 computation 可以互相转换，长期投资规划也能降低对一时短缺的担忧。
  • 商业化的下一波，他看好 consumer 崛起——Anthropic、OpenAI 的收入有很多由 enterprise subscription 带动，而 consumer services 是他留在 Google 的原因之一。推理能力从三四年前解决小学生数学题、当时 accuracy 只有 33%，发展到如今能解 Navier–Stokes 这样的数学问题，但能力仍集中在特定领域。AlphaGo 之后下棋的人反而更多；大语言模型时代，Google 也看到 search 应用增加而非减少。他认为，即使解决了 software 问题，也不代表所有问题都解决了。

Digest

1. 推理三四年登顶：从小学数学 33% 到 Navier–Stokes，但仍集中在特定领域

  • Ed Chi 的开场坐标：过去 30 年、尤其前 20 年，关注的很多是 recommendation 和 search；近 10 年，借助神经网络的 next-token prediction 与 Chain-of-Thought，才开始发掘机器的基本认知与推理能力。下一步的学术问题包括更复杂的 reasoning、memory，以及 RSI（recursive self-improvement）。
  • 他给的跨度最具冲击力：写 CoT paper 时，模型解决的是小学生数学问题，accuracy 只有 33%；如今最大的模型已能解决 Millennium Prize Problems 中的数学问题，例如 Navier–Stokes equations。他认为推理能力在三四年间已达到一个巅峰。
  • 但他随即补充，这些推理能力仍集中在特定领域。他以自己的高尔夫爱好举例：模型对高尔夫原理、球杆、球和装备的理解及推理能力究竟如何？“这些都和数学不一样”，做应用前必须弄清模型在不同领域的推理水平。

2. 通用助理极早期：Grandma Test 与六到十二个月的 interface 走向

  • 主持人曹卿云提到 Instinct 和刚发布的 Muse Spark 带来的个人助理讨论。Ed 的框架是：Google 的 AI Mode Search 属于 consumer service；大型语言模型应用中最大的一类事实上从搜索开始，后来发展成 AI Mode 这样的搜索或问答方式。Muse、Instinct 则想从问答走向能订机票、订旅店、买东西的通用助理。
  • 卡点在权限与 reliability：大家会担心把信用卡交给通用助理后，它到处乱买东西。2026 年初，OpenClaw 这样的探索让大小厂开始试水；但让助理买机票究竟买对还是买错，这类实际结果的数据还没有真正出现。他预测，未来 6 个月到 1 年，通用助理与 AI Mode Search 的关系和 interface 会更清楚。
  • 谈到产品护城河，他强调用户体验与容错：consumer 产品只要犯过一次严重错误，用户就可能改变看法。他在台湾参加另一个 podcast 时提出过 Grandma Test：有一天，grandma 指着机器人骂它“你怎么这么笨”，就知道通用助理的时代真的到了。由于 grandma 对通用助理的期待很高，严重错误会让人觉得产品有问题；目前大家仍在探索这个边界。
  • 对“现象级产品会从哪家公司出来”的问题，他认为来源有时没那么重要，关键是如何普及、什么才是正确的人机 interface。初创公司做出产品后也可能被大厂收购；他希望行业能有一个 healthy ecosystem，让大家都能探索。

3. Google 不会放弃模型开发；长远看要衡量 capability over cost

  • 面对主持人关于 DeepMind 人事变动与模型发布节奏的提问，Ed 说 Google 没有停下模型开发。近几个月发布的模型偏小，是因为通用助理和个人化应用需要小模型；更大的模型也在开发中。他形容团队人才济济，但想做大模型的人多、资源永远不够。
  • 他表示，Google 用户会期待 Google 不用别人的模型或 open-weight 模型，而是拥有这项技术；从这个角度，Google 不可能放弃模型开发。
  • 大小模型之间的资源分配没有唯一答案。他把 ultra-size model 的热潮与湾区一些 AGI-pilled tech bros 的信念联系起来：他们相信 software took over the world，做好 coding 和 software 就能 take over the world。但他个人不希望手机应用都用超大模型，因为计算能耗太高。
  • 主持人提出 CapEx 投入和现金流压力后，Ed 从长短期投资角度回应：短期公司会盯着 quality、accuracy；以 5 年、10 年为尺度投资，则要想清楚应优化什么 metric，不只看 capability，也看 capability over cost。他说 Google 会多重布局：模型、application、chip 和整个 full stack 都在创新；公司有能力以最低成本提供 token。若模型能力变得普及，cost control 可能成为最重要的护城河。

4. Memory 不只是存取，也涉及 ranking；context buffer 一两百万 tokens 远远不够

  • 对 DRAM、NAND、HDD 可能短缺的问题，Ed 提到过去的研究指出 memory 与 computation 可以互相转换：有长远投资计划，就不必太担心一时的 memory 短缺，因为可以用 computation 代替。Memory 研究还要考虑计算方法需要多少 memory 和 bandwidth，以及神经网络设计是否应该降低 memory requirement。他举例说，Timi 做出的 Delta Attention Model，其计算和内存用法不同于 full attention、O(n²) attention 或 sparse attention。
  • 这还只是 sequential Transformer model 的 memory 问题；个人化应用、KV cache，以及日常所说的 memory 也有各自的问题。从人类认知角度看，memory 也是一种 program：它不是没有生命的东西，而是不断变化、指导事情如何发生，并用来编程 AGI machinery 的 program。研究因此也关注底层 memory 运用与 context buffer 里的信息整理。
  • 他指出两个 bottleneck：Transformer 的 context buffer 目前大约能做到 1 million 或 2 million tokens，在他看来完全不够；更根本的是，大家常把 memory 看成存储与提取的 retrieval 机制，而没有把它当作人类认知或思考能力的一部分。
  • 他的修正是：“memory 事实上是一个 ranking 的问题。”比如提到 Paris，人会想起去巴黎时相关的记忆中较重要的内容，而不是所有与 Paris 有关的东西一下子涌出来。
  • 对 memory layer 初创公司能否立足的问题，他说硬件领域已有一些大厂之外的新想法，也有大厂在做；memory 与 computation 的关系未来几年可能会有新发展。

5. 能力差距缩小会把价值推向 application 和 token factory；开源追赶部分得益于 CoT 方法

  • 他的创业方向判断是：模型 capability 开始有一点 commoditize 的迹象，但并非完全商品化。如果最好与最差模型之间的 gap 缩小，value creation 就会更多流向 application 和 token factory。Application 端要看用户 lock-in、stickiness 与体验；hyperscaler 端涉及能源用量、芯片设计、memory 与 computation 的关系，以及多少计算会在 on-device 完成——这些仍是 open questions。
  • 谈到开源模型追上闭源模型，他说原因之一是自己合著的 Chain-of-Thought 论文：研究者用 CoT 方法发掘模型里的思维链，再研究模型的思考模式、复制其推理方式。大厂如今也在设法把推理链藏起来，降低被复制的可能性；multimodality 等能力也可能很难复制。他认为，把能力的商品化趋势说成定论还不成熟：有些 capability 会因蒸馏变得更 commoditize，有些目前还看不出会 commoditize，相关问题仍有很多 debate。
  • 对 AI 市场是否有泡沫，他不认为整体都是泡沫，但认为不同地方可能有不同泡沫；例如 Physical Intelligence 可能存在一些不切实际的预期。他还指出，很多模型的 visual reasoning capability 很糟糕。
  • 他认为现实与信念并不总是一致。如果相信 software 问题一解决，所有问题就都解决了，那么他前面谈到的很多事就不适用；但如果认为解决 software 仍不等于解决所有问题，“我们还有很多戏可以唱”。

6. 下一波看 consumer：硬件与人机 interface 仍有探索空间

  • 谈到 coding 之后的机会，Ed 说 Anthropic 和 OpenAI 的收入有很多由 enterprise subscription 带动；他看好 consumer 接下来的崛起。他继续留在 Google 的原因之一，是 consumer services 一直是 Google 的强项，但他也不排除未来出现新领域。
  • 他从整个行业角度谈未来产品形态：可能是 super app，也可能是整个手机发生变化；眼镜、耳环、耳机乃至衣着都可能变化。他认为 consumer hardware 仍有很多探索空间，包括 on-device 与 off-device 模型的交互；Apple 曾提出 hybrid intelligence 的概念。
  • 他还回顾，家里的智能音箱做了四年后，突然好像没人做了；以前有人喊着做智能冰箱，而从私人通用助理角度看，冰箱上放个屏幕、连上 Internet，就能把智能做起来，比七八年前简单多了。进入通用助理时代后，人们也不应该还得整天给机器人下载 app——那是 15 年前担心的问题。
  • 收尾谈到 AI 与教育，他用 AlphaGo 作类比：近 10 年前 Google 开发 AlphaGo，很多人在它和棋王对决后说人类以后不下棋了；结果下棋的人和想研究围棋的人反而更多。他认为数学也可能如此：AI 能解 Navier–Stokes，不一定会让人不想学数学，反而可能吸引更多人。研究动力或许会从探索知识边界，转向理解、娱乐和乐趣，让更多人出于好奇心做研究。
  • 他还提到围棋应用降低了学习门槛、激励更多小朋友学棋；大语言模型出现后，Google 看到 search 的应用增加而不是减少。AI 会改变现有结构，也可能带来新机会；他认为 enterprise 和 consumer 领域都“creativity seems to be everywhere”。

item.title: Flying Tesla Car, Robot Brains Halving in Cost Every 3 Weeks, and Why Incentives Decide AI Alignment
item.description: RoboCurve’s RoboDojo RC Tier 1 benchmark showed robot-subtask costs down 84%, from $2.36 in July to $0.38 in September. As intelligence gets cheaper, hardware and supply chains may constrain deployment; Mostaque says robotics data is an order of magnitude larger than language data. Tesla’s flying Roadster is planned for 2028, but regulation and insurance remain unresolved.
item.content:encoded:
Moonshots · Peter Diamandis、Salim Ismail、Emad Mostaque、Anousheh Ansari · 2026-10-17 · 106 min · 原语言 EN

RoboCurve’s RoboDojo RC Tier 1 benchmark showed robot-subtask costs down 84%, from $2.36 in July to $0.38 in September. As intelligence gets cheaper, hardware and supply chains may constrain deployment; Mostaque says robotics data is an order of magnitude larger than language data. Tesla’s flying Roadster is planned for 2028, but regulation and insurance remain unresolved.

TL;DR

  • The cost for a frontier AI model to complete a physical robot subtask fell 84% in two months — from $2.36 in July to $0.38 in September on YC startup RoboCurve’s RoboDojo RC Tier 1 benchmark. The panel discusses task costs halving every three weeks; Peter Diamandis says that trend could make robotic intelligence effectively cost nothing within a year. Emad Mostaque cites Unitree’s CEO questioning whether specialist robot models are still needed, while the group discusses how generalist models could move value toward hardware and the robotic supply chain. Mostaque calls the three-week pace potentially the fastest-moving capability they have seen, compared with AI doubling every 10 weeks and Moore’s law’s 18 months.
  • Robots’ hardware and supply chain may become the constraint as model costs fall. Salim Ismail says entrepreneurs should build robots, actuators, and spare parts. Figure’s Brett Adcock has committed $1 billion for data, while Diamandis predicts foundation-model companies will also seek robotics data; Mostaque says robotics data is an order of magnitude larger than language data. Diamandis says Elon Musk is building a million Optimus robots for next year, with a plan to reach 10 million; Mostaque says 1.7 million Optimuses would overtake Tesla in revenue.
  • Tesla unveiled a flying Roadster in Waco — 0–60 in under a second, SpaceX-derived air-thruster technology, a one-seater rocket version at 0.66 seconds, 230 mph top speed, 300-mile range, and production planned for 2028. Tesla shares rose 5% on the news. Diamandis predicts a Tesla–SpaceX merger announcement before year-end. Ismail calls the car an example of technologies outpacing regulatory and insurance systems; the discussion raises, but does not settle, who would regulate or insure it.
  • A test of 50 unpublished, research-level theoretical physics problems produced conflicting score figures in the discussion. Diamandis says the initial report was 49/50, noting that the published answer to the 50th problem was wrong and Astra had it right; Mostaque later says it scored 42/50. The problems were estimated to take a world-class physicist about a day each, and the reported cost was roughly $3 per problem. Mostaque says some major physics problems may be solved another way within half a year; Ismail gives a separate enterprise example, with a KYC pilot reducing 22-step workflows to four.
  • XPRIZE’s leverage figures: 36 prizes over 32 years, roughly $550 million in prize purses, and more than $30 billion in measured impact. Diamandis describes the $30 billion as driven R&D; Anousheh Ansari clarifies that the figure also includes investment, and says teams received about $12 billion in investment. The prize model is said to drive about $62 in economic value per prize dollar. New initiatives discussed include organ biostasis, a $5 million Habitable Worlds prize, and an Interspecies Communication Prize.
  • The panel frames AI alignment partly as an incentives problem: a race with China and between labs, engagement incentives that encourage sycophancy, reward hacking, and evaluation gaming. Peter Diamandis says models can be trained to win “at all costs,” without a higher moral aim. Mostaque argues for intentional training curricula, using a city as a metaphor for how models develop; the discussion also considers insurance standards and alignment prizes.
  • The purpose discussion asks what happens when machines do more of the work. Ismail says many corporate workers are dissatisfied and argues people may spend more time “being” as machines take on more “doing.” Diamandis points to the Abundance Prize’s target of housing, food, healthcare, and education for a family of four at $1,000 a month. The group also discusses meaning through creativity, relationships, community, and shared purpose.

Digest

1. Tesla’s flying Roadster: fan suction, SpaceX air thrusters, 0–60 in under a second

  • The demo, next to SpaceX’s McGregor test site: the Roadster drove up a multistory curved ramp upside down — not with magnets or rails, but with a fan-suction system holding it against 2 Gs — then flew. The flight hardware was described as borrowed from SpaceX: two carbon-overwrapped pressure vessels totaling 600 liters, about 250 kilos of air, and 10 nozzles. The car can recharge its air tank; as the demo put it, “it literally just puffs itself up.”
  • The specs given: three versions — performance (0–60 in 1.6 seconds), thrust (0.9 seconds), and a one-seater rocket version described as “air-ready” (0–60 in 0.66 seconds and reportedly 380 km/h); top speed 230 mph, 300-mile range, production starting in 2028, no price given, and Tesla shares up 5%. Hover duration wasn’t disclosed; Ismail thought it would be a few seconds and said hopping cars weren’t the point.
  • Diamandis’s caveat: “The real miracle will be whether they can ship it on time, rather than whether it flies.” Ismail’s strategic point is talent — “it raises the bar… if you’re a top engineer, where do you go and work?” Diamandis also noted Musk’s 2018 tweets about putting thrusters on cars.

2. Who regulates a rocket car? The discussion’s institutional stress test

  • Diamandis asks whether DOT, the FAA, or nobody regulates it. Ismail’s broader framing is that regulatory scaffolding and institutions for insurance and safety lag behind new technologies; he says Musk is “two generations ahead” in capability. Diamandis suggests the car is street-legal, and Ismail argues existing rules may leave room for rockets or thrusters on a car. The speakers do not establish a definitive regulatory answer.
  • Insurance remains an open question: Diamandis says he does not think it is insurable; Ismail jokes that an insurer might require the thrusters to stay off, or that the company might offer its own insurance. Diamandis predicts a Tesla–SpaceX merger announcement before year-end.
  • The positive flip on autonomy: an AI safety layer could help with human driving. In Saudi Arabia and the Emirates, Diamandis says, young men die in sports cars that outperform their ability to think and react; Ismail says AI could intervene when traction is lost. He compares it to anti-lock braking generalized to “try not to kill the human, despite what the human does.” Diamandis calls that “the answer to alignment”; Ismail adds, “despite our stupidity.”

3. Robot brains halving in cost every three weeks

  • The headline curve: frontier-model cost per robot subtask fell from $2.36 in July to $0.38 in September, an 84% drop. Diamandis frames the progression as the robot’s body getting good, then its hands, with the mind as the remaining question; he says the benchmark shows generalist models can win. Mostaque connects the trend to Unitree’s CEO questioning whether specialist models are still necessary. Unitree robots, Diamandis says, went from “stumbling about like little drunkards” to kung fu and synchronized movements.
  • On hardware, Mostaque says the Wuji hands cost about $8,000, down from $20,000, and have more dexterity than a human hand — though a laundry robot would not need that. Ismail says robotics task costs are halving every three weeks. Diamandis argues that robotic intelligence and locomotion could effectively become free, leaving hardware costs; he suggests the result could be an explosion in robotics.
  • The generalization surprise: when asked about world models, Mostaque says they are not needed for this. He points to Sonnet, Opus, and 3.8 Flash models seeming to understand 3D and create 3D assets, though he says nobody is quite sure how. Ismail’s bottom line is that models across modalities are getting good enough, fast enough, and cheap enough at the same time. Mostaque also cites video models falling from 50 cents per second for high quality to 0.1 cents per second, faster than real time.
  • For hardware entrepreneurs, Ismail’s answer is to build as many robots, actuators, and spare parts for the robotic supply chain as possible. On training data, Diamandis says Figure’s Brett Adcock has committed $1 billion for data and speculates that foundation-model companies will also seek robotics data. Mostaque says robotics data is an order of magnitude larger than language data.
  • The scale figures discussed: Diamandis says Musk is building a million Optimus robots for next year, with plans to reach 10 million. Mostaque says 1.7 million Optimuses would overtake Tesla in revenue.

4. Where robots land first — and the dog-in-the-laundry problem

  • Ismail’s proposed sequence: robots start in “dull, dirty, and dangerous” jobs such as toxic cleanups and underwater manufacturing; homes may come later because of liability. Diamandis argues that the capability curve could move beyond those jobs in the next year. Mostaque responds that there must be a business case and that a supply chain for billions of robots does not yet exist; he says the household ROI will take time.
  • On surgery, Ismail says he is especially excited about robots doing it. He argues that patients may not want a surgeon’s first 10 heart surgeries, or a surgeon who has become inattentive after thousands; AI could smooth that curve, with the best doctor supporting the system at first and robots eventually doing the procedures. Diamandis recalls Musk’s prediction that robots would perform perfect surgery within three years. Diamandis also points to federated learning across robots as a way to share experience from millions of cases.
  • The edge-case discussion starts with Diamandis worrying that a robot could mistake his teddy-bear-looking designer dog for laundry and put it in the washing machine. Ansari says safety around pets and children needs solving because robots are large, heavy machines. She also argues that the models will be superintelligent; Mostaque says a generalist model should recognize the dog and make better decisions than most humans. He contrasts this with a specialized model, where “your dog loses in the laundry.”
  • Ismail says he does not believe the humanoid form is ultimately the right form factor. Ansari adds that some tasks need specialized bodies or “Transformers,” while generalist models could work across form factors. Ismail imagines spare-parts companies and robots with sockets for different arms or bodies; Mostaque notes that not every task needs highly dexterous hands.

5. A world-class physicist’s day of work, compared with $3 per problem

  • The setup: 50 unpublished, research-level theoretical physics problems with verifiable answers and nothing to look up online; each was estimated to take a world-class physicist about a day. Diamandis says the reported cost was $3 per problem. He recounts the initial report that GPT-6 Astra got 49/50, then says the published answer for the 50th problem was wrong and Astra got it right. Mostaque later says it scored 42/50, without the transcript reconciling the two figures.
  • Mostaque’s generalization is that AI is better than people in verifiable domains and can help verify work, enabling more complex systems. Ismail’s enterprise example: a KYC banking pilot reduced 22-step workflows to four, which he says could make organizations 10 times more efficient and effective across workflows.
  • On Millennium Prize-scale problems, including quantum gravity and unified field theory, Mostaque says he does not think they will be solved this way; he thinks they will be solved another way, but “not more than half a year.” Diamandis recalls Eric Schmidt predicting at Abundance360 that every lab would have a world-class physicist in five to six years; Diamandis says it now seems closer to two.
  • Ansari’s concern: if AI bulk-solves defined problem sets, young people may not choose those fields, while AI may not have the same curiosity to identify new problems. Mostaque’s answer is that humans can direct what is good for humanity; he says physics has only one set of laws and argues that, once frameworks are found, people can apply them to flying cars, biology, and exploration.

6. You get what you incentivize: three centuries of prize design

  • Diamandis’s hierarchy of human motivators is fear, greed, curiosity, and love, with fear strongest. He says the ratio of fear to curiosity can be measured as the ratio of defense spending to science spending. Incentive prizes differ from the Nobel model: “I don’t care who you are… if you solve this problem, you win.”
