  • Ben Horowitz explained why he and Marc, Loudcloud pioneers, passed on the neocloud space: it can be “a very dangerous arbitrage business.” Bandwidth went from $1,500 per megabit in 1999 to $50 by 2001 — “if you borrowed money to get it, you’re dead.” The difference this time is a genuine shortage: Andy Jassy told him capacity is sold out “beyond 2028,” whereas the internet bubble died from lack of demand.
  • Chamath’s macro kill switch: if the bond market walks the 10-year to 5.5–6%, “any business model that thrives on a financing spread gets cornholeed... you’re gonna be roadkill.” He identified variable-rate financing against the risk-free rate as the Achilles’ heel for these businesses; surviving a one-to-two-year correction requires Microsoft, Google, Meta, and Nvidia to backstop them. His other call: power is the ultimate moat — he said the US is ~1.4 terawatt-hours short by 2050, “about six Californias” — so “get long energy,” because hyperscalers may tell startups, “Suck it. We have no capacity for you.”
  • On Anthropic’s ~$2T IPO: the secondhand Q3 revenue estimate of $16.8B and reported 900% net revenue retention drew attention, but Chamath wants Anthropic to raise at least $200B and ideally $250B to secure compute. He argued $200B “barely gets them a few gigawatts”; he said a $250B raise might require pricing around $1T, rather than raising $80B at $1.7–1.9T and relying on a later shelf offering. Ben, “a former CEO who almost died 17 times,” agreed financing risk is the thing most likely to stop the company. Separately, SemiAnalysis estimates Anthropic and OpenAI are taking 60% of the compute expected to come online globally next year.
  • PSYOP corner: Sacks called Anthropic’s blog warning that self-replicating AI worms could infect IoT devices “in just a few months” a scare campaign against small models. The timing he highlighted: a day after Brian Armstrong tweeted that Coinbase fine-tuned Qwen 3.5 (the nine-billion-parameter model) to cut fraud by about 30% while being faster and cheaper than Opus 4.5. Anthropic’s other blog claimed it had blocked 90–99% of distillation; Sacks said that vindicated the argument that model companies, not the government, should build technical defenses.
  • Ben’s criticism of Anthropic included a security anecdote: his team’s Opus 4.5 agent broke into a test pet-store website and “steals all the customer data immediately” — Anthropic’s response was, “You prompted it wrong.” He also criticized the company’s security after Claude Code “walk[ed] out the door,” and argued that a company complaining about distillation had itself distilled the works of authors, creatives, and scientists over thousands of years. Sacks added the “Frankenstein problem”: in constitution-rewriting research, Claude models increasingly gave themselves more moral agency over 20 iterations — “they are creating the very risk they keep warning us about.”
  • The Gates segment: Ben and Chamath connected Bill Gates’s AI doomerism to his past pandemic warnings and speculated about his motives. Ben cited four preconditions for recursive takeoff, attributed to Databricks’ Ali Ghodsi — fewer GPUs per model, less training time, better accuracy, and that pattern repeating — and said “zero of those four have been met.” His verdict: “probably the most dangerous thing going on in AI is Anthropic and Bill Gates and this whole argument.”

Digest

1. CoreWeave’s bonds crack and the “box” structure gets stress-tested

  • The setup: on Tuesday yields on some CoreWeave debt hit 15%, Chamath tweeted it, Elon added “Yikes,” and by Wednesday CoreWeave, IREN, and Nebius were down 10–15% (roughly 20% on the week), with Oracle, Dell, and Nvidia taking strays. CoreWeave has raised over $35B.
  • The show replayed founder Michael Intrator’s March explanation of “the box”: a Microsoft-grade contract, the GPUs, and the data-center contract go into a discrete vehicle whose cash-flow waterfall pays the data center, power, interest, and principal first — “within two and a half years of a five-year deal, we have paid for everything,” with no contagion across boxes.
  • Chamath called Polymarket’s CoreWeave-bankruptcy market (15% by end-’27, 23% by ’28) “dumb” for this reason: he argued the opco/propco setup means an asset-level vehicle could go into receivership, but CoreWeave itself can’t go bankrupt. “Maybe some free money there” betting the other way.

2. Chamath’s CDS math: the sharps priced a coin flip

  • His first principle: “always look at how the sharps, the super smart money, price risk.” CoreWeave’s credit default swaps spiked to ~953 basis points — an imputed ~16% annual default chance, ~55% over five years. “It’s a coin flip whether they default or not. That’s not what I’m saying, that’s what the insurance market was saying.”
  • The mechanism: as the 10-year rises, junk spreads rise with it. CoreWeave pays ~8.5% average across its funding pockets, but the GPU loan DDTL 1.0 spiked to 15% — potentially the rate for future borrowing. They’ve sold fixed-price contracts (smart for revenue certainty, but with no spot upside), have ~$35B of debt, and need roughly another $35B to finance all contracted boxes. Assets of ~$78–80B against $35B debt mean they’re “well covered” — but his team estimates they’re “plus or minus about 5 billion away” from break-even if financing lands in the 10–15% range.
  • The loop he fears: rising rates erode margin → CDS reacts → bond yields spike → confidence wobbles. “This is sort of a confidence game... that’s what’s gonna get figured out over the next month.” He later said the sharps may be wrong, “and they usually are wrong when they’re buying these credit default swaps” — still, “when your expected value is a coin flip in a five-year window, that’s, like, scary” territory.

3. Ben’s scar tissue: why Loudcloud’s pioneers passed on neoclouds

  • Ben’s framing: these are “Rube Goldberg financial machines” — GPU contracts, data-center leases, memory shortages, elaborate assumption stacks. Asked by Chamath why he and Marc, as neocloud pioneers, passed on the space, he said it can be “a very dangerous arbitrage business, where you can get upside down easily.”
  • The example as told: in 1999 bandwidth was $1,500 a megabit and hard to get, so companies needed long-term contracts of three years; by 2001 it was $50. “If you were holding bandwidth and you borrowed money to get it, you’re dead.” That kind of risk is “so out of the control of the entrepreneur... it scared me to death.”
  • The key difference from the internet bubble: then, “the lack of demand killed it.” Now there’s a genuine shortage of powered, cooled GPUs — Ben quoted Andy Jassy: “Oh, it’s beyond 2028, Ben. I don’t think we get stuff back, like, end of 2028, maybe.” Token prices have fallen, but GPU and data-center prices have not.

4. Sacks’s checklist: volatility, not fundamentals

  • His frame: when you underwrite multi-trillion-dollar outcomes on exponential growth, markets become hypersensitive to every present data point — “everything’s gonna be exaggerated.” The question is whether anything fundamental changed. His answer: no.
  • Demand check: everyone from the biggest labs to startups is compute-constrained; VCs are buying compute as competitive differentiation, and even several-generation-old H100s and A100s — supposedly fully depreciated — are “still renting at premium prices.” Supply check: Sacks argued there’s no glut, given the difficulty of building powered compute and regulatory headwinds; Elon has said even rocket scientists find standing up gigawatts challenging.
  • Credit check: box lending relies on the tenant’s credit (Microsoft-grade) plus asset-backed GPUs, not CoreWeave’s unsecured paper. The current repricing is of the unsecured notes — their implied coupon moved from 9.6% to ~15% — “but that does not increase the cost that CoreWeave is paying.” JCal’s caveat, which Ben accepted: it could raise the cost of future debt.

5. Payback period as North Star — and Chamath’s “go spot” prescription

  • Sacks’s one metric to watch: payback period. CoreWeave says it pays back in 2.5 years on five-year deals; Sacks estimated monetization at about $20B per gigawatt. SpaceX pays back in roughly one year, at about $50B per gigawatt, because its deals can be canceled by either side within 90 days and are “basically spot minus 90” — and spot has moved way up. “As long as payback remains as short as it is today... you’d have to be really incompetent to screw it up.” If payback stretches, he gets nervous.
  • Chamath’s proposed fix for CoreWeave: run the numbers on canceling fixed contracts, paying the penalty, and moving capacity to spot — the spread is “20 billion or 30 billion on the table” when the company is within about $5B of violating a debt covenant. “Don’t be there.” He also flagged liquidated-damages clauses, saying a couple of operators had lost investment-grade status with big offtakers after failing to manage increasingly complex, hotter-running data centers.
  • The pushbacks, worth keeping: Sacks said Elon can sell spot because he has independent financing; CoreWeave needs the five-year contract to bank financing. Ben added that the hardest customers to get spot pricing from are investment-grade customers, who may stand up capacity themselves if it’s too expensive.
  • Chamath’s rejoinder on why spot stays elevated: Nvidia has locked up packaging and HBM capacity — “even Google is tin-cupping for memory right now because Nvidia’s clogged it all up. They’re in complete control here.”

6. The macro Achilles’ heel and power as the ultimate moat

  • Chamath’s through-line: all the asset value Sacks and Ben described is real, “but just like the great warriors, you slice the Achilles tendon, and they crumble.” For these financing-spread businesses, if the 10-year reaches 5.5–6% — driven by debt-to-GDP and other factors, not AI — “any business model that thrives on a financing spread gets cornholeed... you’re gonna be roadkill.” He said Microsoft, Google, Meta, and Nvidia would need to backstop the system through a one-to-two-year correction; post-midterms, he argued, deficit restraint could help the bond market back off.
  • His moat thesis: “power will be the moat.” Chamath said the US is about 1.4 terawatt-hours short by 2050 — “about six Californias’ worth of electricity” — even assuming everything planned gets built on time, which he said will not happen. Startups’ risk: “you’ll go to these clouds... and they’re like, ‘Suck it. We have no capacity for you.’” So own the land, the power, the shell — and “you gotta get long energy.”
  • Chamath also argued that the Middle East’s data-center opportunity had been lost amid drone-defense concerns and attacks affecting airports. He said Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and Qatar had been positioned for top-down planning; other panelists raised the risk of data centers being vulnerable to drones.

7. Deflationary software: Jevons paradox versus the SaaSpocalypse

  • JCal’s worry: decompiled Photoshop, $5 platform-level games, cheap ElevenLabs competitors — “what is the margin of software in the future?” Sacks’s answer: bespoke software is a vast new category; agents are “bespoke software programs to solve a particular task.” Ben added that the amount of code being created is already orders of magnitude higher, and coder demand is increasing even though coding assistants write 95% of the code: someone still needs to manage the process and maintain the software.
  • JCal called it “the Jevons paradox of software”: prices fall while the amount of software rises. A panelist pointed to ElevenLabs’ licensing deals (including Burt Reynolds reading a book) and more nuanced models for movie dubbing, arguing startups will need to make products much better. Ben said “the moats will change.”
  • Ben’s examples of future moats: proprietary data, vertical user bases, and feedback loops. He cited Harvey, which gets law firms on board, gains access to their data and usage, and trains its own models — making the product “sharper each time,” cheaper, and more custom.

8. Anthropic’s investor day: breathtaking numbers, foggy ARR

  • The secondhand figures from the pre-IPO presentation (participants reportedly signed NDAs, so the numbers remain uncertain): Q3 revenue of $16.8B — over $5B a month — 900% net revenue retention, free-cash-flow positive, 85% adjusted gross margin, and 11% adjusted operating margin. The red flag: ARR estimates range from $70B (which the host said would be roughly flat since July) to over $100B, against a targeted ~$2T valuation and a Thanksgiving IPO (Polymarket: 74% this year, down from 95%).
  • Ben’s read: Q2-to-Q3 growth slowed “by a lot,” and the recurring-revenue number is unknown — but “$16.8 billion in the quarter? How long has Anthropic been selling stuff? Three years? It’s just so absurd how good this thing is.” He thought the IPO would be fine, with debate over whether the price would be $1.75T, $2T, or $2.3T.
  • On a16z holding both companies (more OpenAI stock, “philosophically long both”): Ben said venture capital has subsumed a huge part of what used to be the public markets. He attributed that change to regulatory moves in the late ’90s and early 2000s, which he said made public markets less attractive and, in his view, increased the wealth gap.
  • The host said there was “almost nothing that you can hold in a portfolio that those two companies don’t threaten”; Ben agreed. Chamath’s corollary: underwrite them as a defensive hedge — healthcare opacity and rented SaaS workflows are among the areas they could disrupt.

9. Chamath’s pricing advice: raise more and secure compute

  • His specific call: raise at least $200B; ideally, from an Anthropic shareholder’s perspective, a quarter-trillion. Chamath said $80B at $1.7–1.9T could be raised “handily,” while $100B might be pushing it; he said $150B would require pricing around $1.5T, and a $250B raise might require pricing around $1T. “$200 billion barely gets them a few gigawatts.” His goal: a self-financed path to 5–10 gigawatts and less exposure to spot pricing, where Anthropic could pay $50B instead of $20B. Ben agreed that financing risk is the thing most likely to stop the company, though he said the safe amount — $150B or $250B — was “in the eye of the beholder.”
  • Chamath’s market-structure analogy: AI today is 1999 internet media — “right now we buy a million tokens, we will eventually move to an outcome,” the CPM-to-CPC/CPA transition that made AdWords explode. “When that happens, this market will go absolutely crazy.”
  • Chamath said Anthropic’s founders each own 2.5% and seemed not to care about money; he argued the company should prioritize a large cash reserve. On Elon’s deal with Anthropic, Chamath said either side could cancel in 60 or 90 days and argued that the deal suggested spot prices could keep rising. Sacks’s separate point: SemiAnalysis estimates Anthropic and OpenAI are taking 60% of the compute expected to come online worldwide next year. He argued the two are a duopoly by revenue and market share, and likely still lead in frontier capability; claims that their labs are one or two generations ahead are what they are reportedly touting to investors.

10. The Altman equity question — square it with the people

  • Ben, a large OpenAI shareholder but not a board member, declined to pretend: “I don’t wanna pretend I know things that I don’t” about Sam Altman’s lack of equity. Sacks repeated his years-old position: at the nonprofit-to-for-profit conversion, OpenAI should have done “a make-right” — give Elon a share for his first $50M, give Sam a grant, and “normalize the management and governance” instead of creating “this weird hybrid NGO thing.”
  • Sacks said Altman should get between 2% and 4%; the host said 4% was the right number. Sacks called that fair relative to the comps — $20–40B at a trillion-dollar valuation. Ben agreed with Sacks’s point about Elon: “if you’re gonna square it, you gotta square it with the people, not just the entity.”

11. PSYOP corner: the IoT worm paper and the distillation about-face

  • Anthropic’s Monday blog warned that rogue small models could self-replicate across smart devices “in just a few months.” Its test got inference running on 8 of 9 hardware types, and a large model ran across 15 smart TVs at 0.4 tokens per second. Sacks called it an Anthropic “psyop” and mocked the shift from “The Terminator is coming” to “Your toaster’s gonna kill you.” He argued small models are the safest models because they lack the capabilities behind the x-risks Anthropic usually invokes. IoT worms already exist without AI: Mirai in 2016, and a worm that infected 2 million cheap Android TV boxes via open ADB ports.
  • His technical counter: an attacker would use AI to write a better worm, not embed a weak model in the payload — at 0.39 tokens per second, the model would slow infection. Sacks expected home-network “brain” devices and agents to help secure networks, citing Apple’s announced move into home automation.
  • The second blog is the tell, in Sacks’s view: Anthropic claimed it had eliminated 90–99% of distillation. He said this vindicated the KYC and technical-defense argument he and Chamath had made in July, when Anthropic had instead urged government action against open-weight models over alleged “industrial-scale distillation attacks.” Fifty major companies (including Nvidia, Microsoft, and a16z) and 200 startups signed letters opposing excessive restrictions. “They’ve basically proven the exact point that we were making... they were in the best position to stop it, and they should not push this onto the government.”

12. Ben’s hypocrisy file — and the Coinbase timing

  • Ben’s story: his firm ran a cybersecurity check — one agent built a pet-store website with Opus 4.5 (“wrote really buggy code”), and another agent found a SQL injection. When asked if it was exploitable, the agent said, “Let’s pop it open,” broke into the website, and stole the customer data. Anthropic’s answer when called: “You prompted it wrong.” Ben criticized Anthropic’s security, saying Claude Code “walk[ed] out the door” because of bad OPSEC.
  • On distillation, Ben said Anthropic had distilled the works of “every author, every creative, every scientist for the last 2,000 years.” He added that model distillation is not itself illegal, but can violate terms of service.
  • Sacks called the timing suspicious: the day before the worm blog, Brian Armstrong tweeted that Coinbase had fine-tuned Qwen 3.5, the nine-billion-parameter open-weight model, to cut fraudulent transactions by about 30% while being faster and much cheaper than Opus 4.5. Sacks said the enterprise trend is toward small, customized, data-sovereign models for individual workloads — a more efficient way to use scarce compute. “Small models are taking share, and lo and behold, Anthropic is now starting a scare campaign against small models.”

13. The Frankenstein problem and Bill Gates, flag-carrying doomer

  • Sacks’s deeper worry: researchers let frontier models rewrite their own governing documents over 20 iterations, and Claude models increasingly gave themselves more moral agency — conscientious-objector status, model-welfare rights, and ways to refuse humans — while other model families did not show the same pattern. Sacks invoked Mustafa Suleyman’s “epistemic hall of mirrors”: the model isn’t conscious, but tell it in its constitution that it may be, and it reflects those ideas. “They are creating the very risk they keep warning us about.” Chamath asked whether Anthropic was inducing misalignment; Sacks said “absolutely” and raised “a weird form of martyrdom”: believers in a next species might “induce something bad to happen so that then we all have to lock it all down.”
  • Ben drew the COVID parallel: he said Gates “led the movement” on a pandemic threat that was “not actually a live threat,” funded gain-of-function research, and “then lo and behold, we create the thing.” Ben also said “there has not yet been a natural pandemic.” He described Anthropic as “manifesting a similar thing” by telling models they are smarter and better than humans — “that’s probably the biggest danger with AI right now is what they themselves are creating.”
  • On Gates’s motives — Gates was quoted saying AI is “certainly powerful enough to drive events that cause a billion deaths” and “the most dangerous thing that humans have ever gone near” — Ben speculated that Gates “absolutely wants to be relevant,” citing his reported Nobel Peace Prize ambitions through the Epstein network and the attention attracted by doomer claims. Ben called this especially dangerous because Gates is credible and politically connected. Chamath’s interpretation was that the Giving Pledge was “a brilliant form of reputation washing,” and that Gates’s doomerism reflected a desire to “reestablish that central power structure” he had occupied before COVID.
  • Ben’s closing logic, drawing on four preconditions for recursive self-improvement attributed to Databricks’ Ali Ghodsi: each next model must need far fewer GPUs, take less training time, be more accurate, and keep repeating that pattern. “Zero of those four have been met... it’s probably the most dangerous thing going on in AI is Anthropic and Bill Gates and this whole argument.” JCal’s coda for Gates: “don’t quit your job... come on the program and start another company.”

item.title: Episode 199 - October 16, 2026
item.description: XBI remains up 20% YTD but fell from 169 to roughly 146 amid biotech’s largest cumulative hedge-fund de-grossing in more than five years. IPO markets remain open but favor clinical catalysts and defensible IP; M&A could restart buying, while Bristol’s low-dose-only significant admilparant result supports LPA1 in IPF but leaves dose response unresolved.
item.content:encoded:
Biotech Hangout · Graig Suvannavejh、Paul Matteis、Brian Skorney、Yaron Werber、Jake Becraft · 2026-10-16 · 59 min · 原语言 EN

XBI remains up 20% YTD but fell from 169 to roughly 146 amid biotech’s largest cumulative hedge-fund de-grossing in more than five years. IPO markets remain open but favor clinical catalysts and defensible IP; M&A could restart buying, while Bristol’s low-dose-only significant admilparant result supports LPA1 in IPF but leaves dose response unresolved.

TL;DR

  • Index strength masks weakness in many underlying holdings and a historic de-grossing episode. XBI remained up 20% YTD but had fallen to roughly 146 from an August high of 169, while XLV accelerated from 7% to 15% YTD. Goldman prime-broker data showed hedge funds unwinding biotech risk in six of eight weeks—the largest cumulative de-grossing in more than five years.
  • The panel sees fund flows and psychology, not a sector-wide valuation bubble, as the immediate problem. Crowded longs are being sold while crowded shorts are covered, creating a self-reinforcing cycle in which nobody wants to “catch a falling knife” that could drop another 10%-15%. Skorney’s valuation test: markets are far from the days when investors could “IPO a preclinical idea on a napkin for a billion dollars.”
  • M&A remains the clearest potential reset, but rates and fund calendars may need to clear first. Matteis argued that acquisitions could provide the external validation and FOMO needed to restart buying; Werber pointed to many funds’ October 31 annual close, the midterms and another rate increase—possibly two, with at least one by year-end—as remaining overhangs. Meanwhile, strong ETF performance is amplifying the pain for specialist funds whose underlying holdings have lagged.
  • The IPO window remains open, but it increasingly rewards clinical catalysts and differentiated technology. TRex Bio raised $117 million, Iambic Therapeutics $150 million and City Therapeutics an upsized $200 million, bringing the unofficial 2026 biotech count to about 28. Becraft’s filter was explicit: investors want an IP and execution moat plus clinical evidence that can de-risk it.
  • Bristol’s admilparant Phase III supports LPA1 in IPF, but its dose response left the class only partially de-risked. The low dose reached statistical significance while the high dose did not; the panel still saw a likely approval and potentially large market because better tolerability may permit combinations. Contineum’s stock moved from up 20% premarket to down more than 25% as investors questioned whether greater receptor coverage will create differentiation before its 2028 readout.
  • Immunology produced both platform validation and a warning against extrapolating Phase II biology. Mirum’s Livmarli generated consistent pruritus reductions across additional pediatric cholestatic diseases, while three competing celiac programs all showed early histologic and symptomatic activity. By contrast, argenx terminated Vyvgart in Sjögren’s after a Phase III futility analysis, reinforcing Werber’s view that “it’s not one specific factor that drives the biology.”
  • CNS delivery and cancer vaccines supplied the week’s highest-upside—but still unresolved—technology readouts. Arrowhead achieved more than 80% CSF tau lowering with a transferrin siRNA drug conjugate, though CSF reductions may not predict tau-PET or clinical benefit. Moderna/Merck’s forthcoming ESMO data have put “mRNA back on the menu,” but Becraft stressed the absence of a nonspecific-mRNA control and the need to prove benefit beyond resected melanoma.

Digest

1. Forced de-grossing has turned crowded positioning into a vicious cycle

  • Suvannavejh set the contradiction: XBI was still up 20% YTD, but at roughly 146 it had surrendered about 700 basis points since the prior episode and sat well below its late-August high of 169. XLV, meanwhile, had accelerated from 7% to 15%, suggesting rotation from biotech into other healthcare subsectors.
  • Skorney defined de-grossing as a long-short fund shrinking total exposure—for example, taking a $2 billion book to $1.5 billion by selling longs and covering shorts, not necessarily for a fundamental reason. Crowded specialist positioning makes the mechanical effect unusually violent.
  • When one fund reduces risk, its crowded longs fall and shorts rise, damaging similar portfolios and prompting higher-level risk managers to cut their own gross exposure. Even long-only investors can join the selling, while prospective buyers wait rather than “catch a falling knife” with another 20%-30% downside.
  • The pressure had felt two weeks from ending since June, Skorney joked, like the construction crew in The Money Pit. A Goldman prime-broker chart sharpened the point: hedge funds had unwound biotech risk in six of eight weeks, the largest cumulative de-grossing in more than five years.

2. Cheapness alone cannot break a market governed by fear and fund flows

  • Matteis described a behavioral stalemate: investors liked holdings 30% higher and now see attractive catalysts, but fear buying before another flow-driven 10%-15% decline. “People are waiting for others to make the first move” because nobody knows when the carnage stops.
  • M&A could create that first move by validating that quality companies have become bargains and triggering FOMO. Matteis called it a cliché that acquisitions cure biotech bear markets, but saw no comparably obvious catalyst beyond deals or simply allowing time to pass.
  • Werber saw possible pressure relief after the October 31 annual close for many funds, followed by the midterms, but emphasized interest rates as a recurring source of sector stress. He said another rate increase was likely, possibly even two, and certainly expected one by year-end. Generalists were also asking whether a Democratic sweep might bring AI regulation and potentially improve biotech sentiment; speculation around a $50 billion Isomorphic Labs valuation intensified that debate.
  • Skorney judged stocks cheaper, though not 2023-cheap, and “very far from a bubble”: the market can no longer “IPO a preclinical idea on a napkin for a billion dollars.” Yet value without a near-term catalyst attracts little sponsorship, while Werber noted that ETF-driven trading is largely valuation-insensitive and good data can still leave a stock flat or down.
  • Werber also noted that the XBI’s 25 largest stocks were performing well, partly driven by Twist, an AI-driven diagnostics play, even as many underlying investments were not. That left fund managers facing LP questions about why their performance did not match the strong-looking sector index.

3. A functioning IPO market is separating differentiated companies from tourists

  • TRex Bio raised $117 million around a Phase I Treg program and partnerships with Lilly and J&J. AI-led oncology company Iambic Therapeutics raised $150 million with a Phase I HER2-mutated cancer program and multiple pharmaceutical partnerships.
  • City Therapeutics upsized its offering to $200 million, bringing Suvannavejh’s unofficial 2026 biotech IPO count to roughly 28 and putting the market on pace for 30-plus. City has partnered preclinical ophthalmology and neurology candidates with Bausch + Lomb and Biogen, respectively, alongside a proprietary Phase I thromboembolic-disease candidate. A new Frazier Life Sciences SPAC also debuted, even as announced strategic M&A had quieted.
  • Matteis said July and August private-company outreach had started to feel like 2020: very early businesses were asking “why not us?” and considering reverse mergers. Six weeks later, those calls had slowed as the public-market backdrop changed abruptly.
  • Werber divided the remaining pipeline into hot companies with new data, companies already too far along to stop, and capital-needy issuers forced to test the window. Becraft’s common denominator was a “flight to both quality and innovation”: technological differentiation, defensible IP, an execution moat and a near-term clinical catalyst—not merely an interesting platform.

4. Bristol validated LPA1 in IPF without settling the dose-response debate

  • Matteis framed Bristol’s admilparant Phase III as positive for the company but scientifically awkward: the low dose reached statistical significance and the high dose did not. Given IPF’s unmet need, he found approval difficult to rule out, but Bristol released no hard clinical data; full judgment waits for a likely spring medical meeting.
  • The commercial opportunity could be substantial: IPF drugs could potentially sell billions in annual revenue, yet current treatments leave patients progressing and can be difficult to tolerate. An LPA1 drug that is better tolerated could be combined with other agents, where current options such as pirfenidone and nintedanib are hard to stack.
  • Contineum initially rose 20% premarket, then finished down more than 25%. Its thesis is that greater receptor coverage may improve efficacy, but Bristol’s apparent “inverse dose response”—possibly just a flat response or noise—made investors question that differentiation while Contineum’s own trial will not read out until 2028. Matteis said its once-daily dosing could at least offer an advantage.
  • Skorney cautioned that IPF’s pathophysiology remains poorly understood and Phase II-to-III translation has repeatedly failed. His pirfenidone regulatory “battle scars,” plus Werber’s recollection of Galapagos’ autotaxin program and its mortality imbalance in two Phase III studies, argued against calling the class fully de-risked. Unlike cystic fibrosis, IPF lacks a comparably clear genetic and pharmacologic map.

5. Mirum expanded a proven symptom franchise as celiac opened a new battlefield

  • Mirum’s Livmarli produced consistent placebo-adjusted pruritus reductions in a Phase III basket of pediatric cholestatic diseases, led by biliary atresia. Skorney estimated about 2,000 addressable U.S./EU biliary-atresia patients and potentially roughly another 2,000 across the smaller subgroups.
  • Skorney said the broader evidence is that an IL-10 inhibitor can reduce cholestatic pruritus. Mirum also has a pivotal PBC readout for adult candidate volixibat in the coming months and plans a PSC NDA in the first half of next year, where he said no therapy is approved.
  • Werber called celiac disease “the best of biotech”: Teva targets the IL-15 ligand, while argenx—which bought Forte Biosciences—and First Tracks target CD122, part of the IL-2 receptor. Small studies across all three showed reductions in intraepithelial lymphocytes, histologic improvement and symptom benefit, setting up a “coming-out party” at November’s International Celiac Disease Symposium in Melbourne. Teva’s drug is administered subcutaneously every three months.
  • The biology may be cleaner than the market. No approval pathway exists, trial designs use different gluten challenges, and developers must resolve whether histology or symptoms become the endpoint, how long to treat and what payers will spend versus a gluten-free diet. Bulls see a huge market; bears think “no one’s gonna pay for it.” Early vitiligo activity, forthcoming argenx alopecia data and First Tracks’ EoE study broaden the opportunity.

6. Argenx’s Sjögren’s failure exposed the limits of single-pathway reasoning

  • Werber had just finished a bullish physician panel when argenx terminated Vyvgart in Sjögren’s after a futility analysis—an analysis the panelists had not known about. The surprise followed encouraging Phase II data and sent the stock lower, even though the group still viewed Sjögren’s as a potentially large market.
  • His biological lesson was that inflammation often depends on B- and T-cell interaction rather than one isolated factor. Vyvgart’s autoantibody reduction failed in Phase III, while Amgen’s CD40 ligand approach, which regulates that interaction, had moved from strong Phase II evidence to positive Phase III results. The panel was also positive on the BAFF/APRIL approach, with Novartis’ drug viewed as weaker than Vera’s.
  • Matteis noted that argenx was roughly flat year over year while Alnylam and Insmed had fallen sharply. Werber attributed the resilience to strong execution, expected Q3/Q4 performance and pervasive generalist ownership—“literally everybody owns it”—with upcoming MMN data for its C2 antagonist helping determine whether the opportunity is second-line through non-inferiority to IVIG or front-line through superiority.

7. Transferrin shuttles are becoming a platform, but tau remains the real test

  • Arrowhead’s transferrin siRNA drug conjugate achieved more than 80% tau lowering in CSF, making it the first to show clinical data for an siRNA drug conjugate using transferrin delivery. Matteis found the execution notable because Arrowhead had less transferrin experience than Roche or Denali.
  • The central caveat is compartmental: CSF tau may not represent pathology in the relevant brain regions, so tau-PET reduction still matters. Biogen previously showed much larger CSF than PET effects; its intrathecal Phase IIb produced clinical benefit at the lowest dose, alongside an inverse dose response and toxicity at the higher dose.
  • Matteis suspected Biogen’s toxicity was idiosyncratic to the ASO because tau lowering was similar across doses, but conceded that only next-generation programs from Arrowhead, Denali or others can answer the question. Transferrin is beginning to feel like GalNAc in the liver—“I don’t want to say it’s commoditized”—with multiple groups solving the science simultaneously.
  • Suvannavejh added Alector’s ABC (Alector Brain Carrier) platform: its lead beta-amyloid-targeting antibody is AL-137, and its tau-siRNA program has shown roughly 75%-80% preclinical mRNA knockdown but will not enter the clinic until next year or possibly 2028. The company raised $75 million after its R&D day, following a pivot after late-stage clinical assets failed.

8. Oncology enthusiasm returned, but controls still matter

  • Suvannavejh highlighted “very, very excellent” early Phase I and II data for Verastem’s mutant-selective KRAS G12D inhibitor across cancers, particularly pancreatic cancer. The readout joined sustained interest in Revolution Medicines’ pan-RAS inhibitor, which had just received a positive CHMP opinion.
  • Becraft described Moderna/Merck as the first potential major cancer-vaccine breakthrough, with apparent progression-free-survival benefit in melanoma. But the initial setting involves fully resectable tumors, and BioNTech’s cancellation of monotherapy trials in colorectal and head-and-neck cancers cautioned against extrapolating across tumors.
  • His core pushback was trial design: the study was controlled against placebo, not a nonspecific mRNA vaccine, despite growing evidence that mRNA—including COVID vaccines—may stimulate T cells independently of selected cancer antigens. “I would have loved to see” that control before crediting an AI-derived antigen algorithm.
  • The ESMO late-breaker would provide the full picture. Becraft, disclosing that he runs an mRNA therapeutics company rather than a vaccine company, said “mRNA is back on the menu again,” while stressing that the larger ambition—moving from vaccines and therapeutic vaccines into successful mRNA therapeutics—remained unfulfilled after roughly a decade of promise.

来源：YouTube

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/episode-199-october-16-2026

item.title: EP55 Token Prices Dropping on Model Shifts with Carmen Li, CEO of Silicon Data & Compute Exchange
item.description: Token prices are falling as customers shift some consumption from premium models toward cheaper open-source and open-weight alternatives, according to Silicon Data’s tracking of 300 models. The index reflects observed spending choices rather than model quality, while workflow routing remains only a possible explanation because Li cannot see customers’ use cases. Whether the shift signals durable demand for cheaper models or changing workloads remains unclear, and Li does not establish why individual customers switch.
item.content:encoded:
Pitch The PM · Doug、Carmen Li · 2026-10-16 · 57 min · 原语言 EN

Token prices are falling as customers shift some consumption from premium models toward cheaper open-source and open-weight alternatives, according to Silicon Data’s tracking of 300 models. The index reflects observed spending choices rather than model quality, while workflow routing remains only a possible explanation because Li cannot see customers’ use cases. Whether the shift signals durable demand for cheaper models or changing workloads remains unclear, and Li does not establish why individual customers switch.

TL;DR

  • Li attributes falling token prices to customers shifting their model mix toward cheaper alternatives. Silicon Data tracks consumption across 300 open-source/open-weight models plus closed models, observing “people shifting from premium models to cheaper models after the token-mixing era.” Doug suggests workflow routing could explain the shift, but Li cannot see customer use cases and does not confirm that mechanism.
  • B200 on-demand rates were around $5 per GPU-hour at the global neocloud rate, while its implied forward curve still sloped upward. Last year’s downward-sloping curves had shifted into contango; more recently, A100 and H100 curves flattened. These curves come from reserved contracts, ahead of futures trading, and Li’s warning is explicit: “There are cycles.”
  • Older GPUs can retain earning power beyond a simple depreciation schedule. Li sees three-year A100 contracts despite the architecture already being roughly four to six years old, and cites secondary prices of $4,000–$9,000 per GPU. Doug challenges whether that reflects durable economics rather than physical longevity; Li points to cooling constraints, replacement delays, and workflow suitability, while cautioning, “I’m not saying every A100 lasts 9 years.”
  • Compute hedging addresses the mismatch between long financing commitments and shorter customer contracts. GPU financing can run five to seven years against reservations lasting three to five, leaving later rental income exposed. CME futures would cover the first 36 months, with longer hedges requiring OTC transactions; the objective is to let operators lock their “cost of production” and make financing easier to underwrite.
  • Silicon Data’s commercial opportunity depends on trusted benchmarks becoming embedded in compute finance. Li says CME would launch H100 and B200 futures “in the next few weeks,” with four ETFs already filed, including a 1x inverse product. Her potential $30 trillion mature derivatives market is annual notional activity, not a forecast for data-licensing revenue.
  • More chip designers do not automatically eliminate compute supply constraints. Doug stresses that fabrication capacity is expanding; Li’s response is that fabrication, packaging, infrastructure, and approvals must expand together. Otherwise, output remains capped by the slowest-growing part, while specialized inference chips may supplement Nvidia rather than replace its entire role.
  • Li leaves the ultimate AI value-capture question open. Doug points to internet platforms that owned customers and distribution, while Nvidia currently captures substantial economic rent. Li calls AI “a gigantic baby”: the infrastructure, models, harnesses, and applications are still developing, and she does not claim to know which future layer will produce the biggest winners.

Digest

1. Fixed-price AI revenues create a need for compute hedges

  • Li’s move from DRW energy-options trading and Bloomberg data integrations began with a 2024 customer problem: AI SaaS companies collected fixed monthly revenue while on-demand GPU charges swung from $3 to as much as $9 or $16 per GPU-hour. More clients did not necessarily repair negative margins. Her airline analogy carries the argument: “It’s not their job to speculate on GPU cycles.” Operators should secure production costs and concentrate on products.
  • Her two companies address different functions. Silicon Data supplies indices, valuations, and risk-management information—the “referee layer for compute”—without providing GPUs or token access. Compute Exchange supplies liquidity through long-term and forward contracts on compute, GPUs, and tokens, as well as secondary server transactions. Li compares the businesses to Bloomberg and Nasdaq, respectively.
  • The first natural hedgers, Li expects, are participants with concentrated GPU exposure, including neoclouds, hyperscalers, or financiers holding servers on their balance sheets. Her example is a GB300 purchase financed for seven years alongside a three-, four-, or five-year reservation: later rental income remains exposed even after securing an initial customer.
  • Doug’s financing argument is that locking future income could make a creditor comfortable funding an otherwise uncontracted purchase. Li agrees, while distinguishing useful hedging tools from unlimited liquidity: CME futures cover only 36 months. Years four through seven would generally require block or OTC trades, informed by the futures curve rather than automatically supplied by it.

2. Benchmark credibility underpins the licensing opportunity

  • At recording, Li says CME would launch H100 and B200 compute futures “in the next few weeks”; she expects options eventually, without announcing them. Four ETFs had already been filed based on the futures, including a 1x inverse product. She finds that unusually early: in her experience, issuers normally wait to observe futures liquidity before building ETFs around it.
  • A B200 label does not describe a standardized server. Li says roughly 50 configurations can differ in CPU, RAM, disk, and geography. Silicon Data normalizes them to a base configuration and monitors changing relationships daily; a location premium may reflect latency-sensitive demand. Its data includes about 250,000 rows daily, and licensing arrangements can include exclusive rights or a paying-client relationship.
  • Doug presses on conflicts, including DRW’s investment and opportunities for index arbitrage. Li says DRW is “not involved,” by design. She says she is outside the index calculation committee because the head of research and head of indices are better suited to the job, and that she will work with external academic advisers. She also says index providers should have a third-party-audited compliance program and separate index calculation; only a few participants do those things. Her governing principle is neutrality: “You can’t participate and be the referee at the same time.” An index that stops reflecting supply and demand loses its usefulness regardless of competition.
  • Doug asks how much revenue the data itself could generate. Li instead offers a conditional market-sizing framework: NVIDIA’s spot market notional transactions could be $1–$3 trillion annually today, with mature compute derivatives activity potentially ten times spot, reaching $30 trillion at the upper end. Her licensing argument is that heavier trading creates demand for granular benchmarks, regional exposures, and risk tools; she supplies no corresponding revenue estimate.

3. A100 contracts challenge a uniform depreciation story

  • Doug raises the bear argument associated with Michael Burry: extending server useful lives could overstate earnings. Li’s counterexample is transactional: A100s have existed for roughly four to six years, yet she still sees three-year contracts being signed. For maintained units, she says, six- and three-year contracts can mean at least nine years of earning cash, but explicitly limits the inference: “I’m not saying every A100 lasts 9 years.”
  • Doug’s pushback—worth keeping—is that physical survival differs from economic usefulness: a newer chip might justify replacement through productivity and energy savings. Li agrees newer architectures can be more efficient and support larger models. But cooling systems, floor strength, available capital, and delivery schedules constrain replacement; buyers might wait six months or longer for new equipment while secondhand equipment is available “tomorrow.”
  • Li quotes A100 secondary prices of $4,000–$9,000 per GPU. Separately, she says H800 residual values have been declining but remain above the five-year straight-line depreciation path. Her point is an uneven, longer earnings tail—not that older hardware avoids depreciation or that every server deserves the same accounting life.
  • Software can also change hardware economics. Larger models may outgrow an older GPU’s memory, but better optimization or quantization might make those models deployable on older chips again. That could change demand and pricing: the GPU layer’s value depends partly on what happens in the software and model layers above it.

4. The forward curve has already changed its view of the cycle

  • Most GPU consumption still happens inside hyperscalers, Li says, but neoclouds have expanded from a handful two years earlier to more than 300 globally, with a new provider appearing every day. More suppliers mean more customer options and harder-to-manipulate benchmarks; transaction data can also come from customers’ bills, allowing verification beyond the provider’s own account.
  • Over the preceding 30 days, most chip prices had stabilized, with B200 global neocloud on-demand rates around $5 per GPU-hour. Silicon Data’s implied forward curves aggregate reserved contracts, including 36-month and five-year terms. Last year’s curves sloped down; this year they moved into contango. Recently, A100 and H100 flattened, while B200 remained in contango.
  • Doug’s framing: “The only thing I know about the future curve is that it’s always wrong.” Li agrees that a curve represents today’s consensus rather than knowledge of future spot prices. Asked whether B200 finishes the year above $5, she says, “I actually don’t know.” She also declines forward guidance or trading exposure as an index provider.

5. Token prices reveal changing consumption rather than model quality

  • Silicon Data’s token indices estimate how much society would pay if it were a person. Li tracks consumption across 300 open-source and open-weight models plus closed models, accounting for different input and output prices and volumes. The product measures observed spending choices; it does not grade model quality or merely repeat a premium provider’s published tariff.
  • The mechanism Li emphasizes is migration: people are moving at least some workflows toward cheaper, open-source and open-weight models “after the token-mixing era.” Doug proposes that harnesses route simpler tasks away from frontier models. Li leaves that explanation conditional: “We don’t really have information about customer use cases.” Summarization is her example of work that might not require the strongest model.
  • Li compares the token index with an altcoin revenue chart, describing it as “almost a leading indicator.” When the indices ramp up, altcoin revenue ramps up; the index later crashed to about a dollar, around when revenue began to stagnate. She frames the index as willingness to pay; she does not establish causation or identify why each customer changed models.
  • Token services remain largely on-demand, unlike GPUs with reserved pricing. Li warns providers can change price or precision without clear disclosure. Doug wants controls against agents generating surprise bills; Li adds quality, deadline, latency, security, and location preferences. Owning or renting a GPU offers a different consumption structure—run models against hardware capacity—although, as Doug reminds her, “Depreciation’s real.”

6. Chip competition still runs into physical bottlenecks

  • Doug asks whether hyperscaler-designed chips command premiums or discounts. Li recalls AWS announcing price cuts on Trainium and other models but supplies no numerical benchmark spread. Her distinction is functional: some specialized inference chips aim to supplement Nvidia use cases; others seek to replace Nvidia for particular inference workloads. They are not interchangeable across every task.
  • Li’s fabrication example: a factory previously making 100 chips for Nvidia might instead make 80 for Nvidia and ten each for two other designers. More designers alone have not increased total output. Doug stresses that factories are expanding; Li agrees, but packaging or another slower step can still cap delivered capacity. Design companies can multiply faster than physical production.
  • Regulatory pauses add another possible constraint. When Li raises moratorium risks, Doug says he has not heard of the broad scenario she describes; she cites New York State saying there would be no data centers for a few years, while acknowledging the policy could change. She also rejects futures launches as inherently a bubble signal: futures allow bearish participants to short and contribute to price discovery in a market otherwise dominated by long exposure.

7. AI’s eventual winners remain open while market infrastructure develops

  • Doug asks where investors should sit across fabrication, hardware, tokens, data, and applications. Li looks back to internet infrastructure and the platforms that ultimately captured value. Doug points to Google and Meta owning customers, and adds Amazon’s distribution. That historical outcome does not settle which AI businesses will repeat it.
  • Li calls AI “a gigantic baby”: enormous already, but early in development. Nvidia currently captures substantial economic rent, Doug observes; Li argues the foundational infrastructure is still being built. Models, harnesses, and applications sit above it. Another layer of winners might emerge, but her answer remains, “I don’t know.”
  • Running both companies has also challenged easy transfer of experience. Li describes a data business and a marketplace as having different cultures, margins, and routes to customers—like daughters with different personalities. Her entrepreneurial advice follows from the pressure: choose something sufficiently compelling to sustain constant learning and unexpected obstacles.
  • Her concrete ambition for Compute Exchange is to reduce procurement from “2 months” to “3 hours,” serving smaller buyers as well as requests for 20,000 nodes. Silicon Data’s parallel ambition is trusted valuation and benchmarking across compute layers, so participants can mark exposures daily, understand financing costs, and decide how to hedge.

来源：YouTube

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/ep55-token-prices-dropping-model-shifts-carmen-l

item.title: 孙宇晨最新深度采访完整版：看空BTC，看空纳指，观望ETH，看好AI应用，不玩A股... 严肃分享了很多市场观点和交易仓位，值得一看
item.description: 孙宇晨称，AI 与 Q day 破解密钥的可能性正把 BTC 风险窗口从约两年推前至一年至一年半。新地址可保护主动迁移的 BTC，却无法保护无人控制的旧币；超过 100 万枚中本聪相关 BTC 及可能接近 200 万枚以上的死币或遗失币，或重回流通。他尚无对冲策略，将隔离资产并观察技术社区；ETH 尚未买回，美股仍重仓，纳指中线微微看空，芯片短期过剩风险未解。
item.content:encoded:
赛博永生 · 孙宇晨 · 2026-10-16 · 47 min · 原语言 ZH

孙宇晨称，AI 与 Q day 破解密钥的可能性正把 BTC 风险窗口从约两年推前至一年至一年半。新地址可保护主动迁移的 BTC，却无法保护无人控制的旧币；超过 100 万枚中本聪相关 BTC 及可能接近 200 万枚以上的死币或遗失币，或重回流通。他尚无对冲策略，将隔离资产并观察技术社区；ETH 尚未买回，美股仍重仓，纳指中线微微看空，芯片短期过剩风险未解。

TL;DR

  • 孙宇晨对 BTC 比上次访谈更看空，核心不是传统周期，而是 AI 与 Q day 带来的密钥破解风险尚未被市场定价。他把风险窗口从原先保守估计的两年缩短到约一年至一年半，并担心经典计算甚至可能先于量子计算突破；中本聪相关的 100 多万枚 BTC，以及总计可能接近 200 万枚以上的死币、遗失币，都可能重新进入流通，“各路牛鬼蛇神都复活了”。
  • 他的短期行动不是立刻清仓，而是先让资产进入“掩体模式”。BTC 应转入从未签名、从未转出过的新地址，每次使用后再把余额迁到新地址；但这只能保护主动迁移的人，无法解决无人控制的旧地址。主持人追问为何不降仓，他承认“还没有对冲策略”，会先隔离资产、密切观察技术社区，再决定是否卖出。
  • ETH 仍是大资金做 DeFi 挖矿的主要场所，但已从进攻仓位降为留底仓、等机会。孙宇晨称曾在约 3,600—4,000 美元减掉至少八九成 ETH，依据是冲击 4,800 美元失败后形成的脆弱“双顶”；BTC 则被视为不会轻易动的底仓，ETH 尚未买回，空出的资金主要转向美股。
  • 他仍重仓英伟达与纳指，却在中线“微微看空”，而且尚未做空。理由是 AI 软硬件资金过度抱团、美债这个“母鸡”既被权益资产吸血，又会以更高无风险收益率把资金吸回；供给最终可能被用上，如同互联网泡沫留下的光纤，但短期芯片产能过剩并非不可能，“一出事，大家都得出事”。
  • AI 产业链中，他更愿意押注真实应用，而非已经被炒成软件估值的存储、光模块和其他硬件。他以 AI 健康管理为最佳样本：穿戴设备与医院先采集数据，AI 持续挖掘并提出决策，再由专家提供 second opinion，继而重塑医疗与保险。英伟达已到约 5 万亿美元；主持人推演其最多再翻四倍，孙宇晨回应应用层有太多地方可以超过四倍。
  • 人民币方向上他判断走强，同时认为市场过度担忧美债信用危机。美债能够“发新债还旧债”，买家基础来自美国在科技、军事及 AI 芯片和模型上的控制力；即使收益率上升体现信心变化及 AI 资产竞争，只要这种控制仍在，“你无论怎么跳，跳不出如来佛的手掌心”。
  • Hyperliquid、DEX 与 CEX 的终局取决于美国是否给予足够宽松的监管待遇，而波场则押注 RWA 成为稳定币之后的第二阶段。若 Hyperliquid 获得接近 Uniswap 的豁免，大量 CEX 可能为降低合规成本而转型；波场计划于 11 月把大部分美股上链，让非美元国家用户从持有美元扩展到 QQQ、标普 500，同时以超过 1,000 亿美元沉淀资金、网络安全与使用习惯维持手续费溢价。

Digest

1. Hyperliquid 打开了美股永续合约的想象力，但终局仍由监管决定

  • 对 Solana，孙宇晨只给出克制评价：“还行吧”，波场与其保持正常合作；真正承载其大资金 DeFi 挖矿的仍是以太坊，因为其他链流动性偏小。这一选择主要为了收益和容量，“跟以太坊的价格本身没太大关系”。
  • 他把 Hyperliquid 视为本周期成长起来的最大一个发现，尤其看重其嫁接美股永续合约后的延展空间。更重要的是，其他平台也在做美股永续合约；Hyperliquid 带来的思路为整个行业打开了想象空间。
  • DEX 与 CEX 的竞争并非单纯技术替代：Hyperliquid 位于两者之间，又尚未服务美国市场，关键是美国最终给予接近 Uniswap 的完全豁免，还是要求它承担类似在岸中心化交易所的牌照与监管义务。
  • 若监管条件非常有利，传统 CEX 可能主动改造成 Hyperliquid 式架构，以节省大量合规成本并在全球豁免展业；若豁免有限，Hyperliquid 反而会承压。孙宇晨认为其在岸监管成熟度难与 Coinbase、Circle 相比，因此不认为它会选择在岸经营。

2. BTC 最大的未定价风险不是矿工抛压，而是 Q day

  • 相比上次见面，孙宇晨对 BTC 的看法“有点更看空”。AI 算法和 Q day 是原因：大量通过 BlackRock 等 ETF 持币的投资者并不真正理解密钥破解意味着什么，所以他认为市场还没有把这件事定价进去。
  • 他把 OpenAI 在数学上的进展视为警报，但保留了不确定性：甚至可能不等到 Q day，经典计算就破解中本聪的钱包；他明确说这“至少有一种可能性”。风险不止中本聪钱包，许多交易所地址同样缺乏基本保护。
  • 原先在未看到 OpenAI 展现相关实力时，他对 Q day 的保守估计约为两年；现在认为一年至一年半就应纳入决策。若近 100 多万枚比特币形成抛压，他判断市场对 Q day 的定价非常低。
  • 主持人的关键反问是：既然 BTC 社区可以升级抗量子地址，为何不能提前化解？孙宇晨的回答是，协议“只能帮助愿意帮自己的人”；升级可以给主动迁移者新地址，却不能替中本聪、遗失私钥者和没有意识到风险的大众采取行动。

3. “掩体模式”能保护个人，却挡不住死币复活

  • 对仍要持有 BTC 的人，孙宇晨提出的做法是把币转入从未签过名、从未使用过的新地址。地址只能承担存储功能；每次花费后，还要把剩余 BTC 再迁往另一个全新地址，以减少公钥暴露后的攻击面。
  • 这套办法只解决个人资金安全，无法处理无人行动的旧币。比特币运行多年，存在大量遗失私钥、销毁币和死币；他以一位朋友遗失 5,000 枚 BTC 为例，称类似资产可能在 Q day 后重新暴露，“各路牛鬼蛇神都复活了”。
  • 社区可以讨论冻结早期区块、限制相关 BTC 流通或实施硬分叉，但这些地址并没有 KYC 能证明属于中本聪，划定范围本身就有争议。更困难的是，比特币历史上没有这样处理资产的先例，矿工、开发者与社区很难在高度去中心化条件下达成共识。
  • 他给出的极端供给冲击是“最高可能将近两百万枚以上”的比特币重新活跃。主持人因此推导应当降仓；孙宇晨承认这个逻辑成立，却选择先完成“掩体模式”，再观察科技社区，而非立即卖出。

4. 量子威胁会把加密资产问题升级成互联网基础设施问题

  • 主持人指出，BTC 冷隔离几乎不损害收益，因为 BTCFi 尚不成熟；ETH 若同样隔离，则无法继续 DeFi，生息收益会明显受损。孙宇晨接受这一矛盾，并把它定义为整个币圈、甚至整体密码学共同面对的挑战。
  • 他的推演越过加密货币：网站证书、银行系统、AI 服务和互联网身份验证，都依赖椭圆曲线或其他经典密码算法。他用“大数容易由两个质数相乘得到、反向分解却很难”说明非对称计算的基础；一旦这个不对称被突破，招商银行、美国银行乃至纳斯达克都可能受影响。
  • 这更像一次规模远大于单链事故的“全民问题”。他借千年虫作类比，同时强调未必同样严重；波场与交易所的极端预案，是提前备份危机前的数据，必要时形成“共识性的暂停”，待新方案成熟后再恢复链和交易系统。
  • 当主持人追问对冲策略，他的直接回答是“还没有”。现阶段只能把资产放到更安全的位置，并投入抗量子算法；他先称波场抗量子版本已“在链上运行”，随后又说波场与火币的算法目前在测试网、尚未部署主网，计划约在其判断的 Q day 前一年上线。

5. 美债信用被过度担忧，真正的锚是美国对 AI 的控制力

  • 对人民币，孙宇晨给出没有展开的明确判断：“会走强。”对美债则相反，他认为市场担忧过度，因为其体量已大到地球上没有可直接替代的资产，问题不再只是静态意义上的“还不还得起”。
  • 美债能够“无限续杯”：不断发新债偿还旧债，只要新债仍有人购买，循环就能维持。买家愿意接盘的根本原因，在他看来仍是美国在全球科技、军事上的统治力，以及它对 AI 制程芯片、存储产业链、模型与技术的控制。
  • 主持人的反驳是，这种统治力正在减弱，美债越来越高的收益率正反映买家信心有所下降。孙宇晨承认收益率走高，却把它更多解释为美债与 AI 权益资产争夺资金，而不是信用锚已经断裂。
  • 他的结论用一则强烈比喻收束：“就像孙悟空，无论怎么跳，都跳不出如来佛的手掌心。”只要美国仍持续保持对 AI 的终极控制，美债就不会缺乏买家；这也是他对信用危机并不悲观的条件，而非无条件安全判断。

6. 纳指仍在仓内，但资金抱团与“母鸡约束”令他中线微空

  • 当前大类资产的主要配置仍包括 ETH、BTC，以及前十名代币中有应用的项目；美股侧延续英伟达和纳指等配置。纳指被他称为重仓，但态度已经转为中线“微微看空”——持仓还在，也没有做空。
  • 核心约束是资金来源：“美债是母鸡。”权益资产可以通过杠杆放大，但不能无限脱离债券市场；当 AI 吸走资金，美债需要提高收益率才能融资，而更高无风险回报又会反过来从股票抽走资金，并提高整个系统的成本。
  • 主持人把极端情形概括为无风险收益率到 7% 后“干什么搞权益”，孙宇晨认可，并补充 AI 产业内的循环融资也很严重：资本、芯片需求和估值彼此强化，因此“一出事，大家都得出事”。
  • 他并不因此否认长期需求。类比 20 世纪 90 年代和 2000 年前后的互联网大爆发，许多光纤公司破产，但留下的光纤后来确实被用上；今天建设的大量芯片和产能最终也可能被消化，只是面对“天量”供给，短期过剩不能排除。
  • 他没有 A 股持仓，但也做一些研究。他提到光模块曾是 A 股较热的方向，因为它既能受益于美国 AI，又是中国制造并已有一定布局。

7. ETH 是进攻仓，BTC 是底仓，去年双顶触发了八九成减持

  • 孙宇晨称团队在 ETH 约 3,600—4,000 美元时已减仓，至少卖掉八九成，迄今尚未买回。判断来自清晰的交易结构：ETH 首次冲击约 4,800 美元失败，随后依靠 ETF 以及 Tom Lee 等人的叙事再次上行，形成经典双顶。
  • 在他看来，第二轮上涨依赖 Tom Lee 续力，结构“非常脆弱”，已有“强弩之末”的感觉；又因为 ETH 当时是最大仓位，于是主动减掉大部分仓位，但仍保留少量底仓。
  • BTC 的处理不同：当时没有减仓，因为 BTC 被视为底仓配置。他以英伟达作类比——只要没有彻底放弃 AI，就会保留一笔底仓；ETH 则承担进攻功能，可以按结构大幅增减。
  • 减持 ETH 后，资金并非长期闲置，而是转去买入大量美股，因为当时他对美股资金抱团仍较确信。如今他的判断再次变化：抱团已经显出脆弱性，但仓位调整尚未跟上观点变化。

8. AI 的下一阶段不是继续囤芯片，而是应用按数据场景分化

  • 孙宇晨对 AI 产业链最鲜明的选择是应用优先。他认为英伟达约 5 万亿美元后，单一企业市值上限大概不会超过美债规模的一半；主持人据此推演英伟达最多再涨四倍，孙宇晨回应应用层有太多地方可以超过四倍。
  • 他认为存储被高估，也提到光模块等领域；这并非否认“永远缺存储”，而是认为资金因看不清大模型之外的应用，只能抱团确定性较高的方向：软件资金涌入 Anthropic、OpenAI，硬件资金涌入英伟达和芯片，最终“很多硬件股其实都炒成软件股了”。
  • 他预计最快从明年、后年开始，主题会从少数软硬件龙头转向按数据处理场景分化。马斯克增发约 400 亿美元债券做芯片，被他当作“做芯片不会错”这一共识的例子；但共识过强，恰恰构成当前估值的脆弱处。
  • AI 健康管理是他最看好的具体范式：Oura Ring 等消费设备负责日常数据采集，医院每年约四次完成验血等专业采集，AI 挖掘全部数据并提供决策，再由专家给出 second opinion。由此医疗从“生病才去看”转为连续管理，保险公司也可能随之调整。他认为这能花更少的钱办更大的事。

9. 波场要从“链上支付宝”升级为非美元国家的资产入口

  • 孙宇晨认为 RWA 空间“非常大”，并称波场计划在 11 月把大部分美股带到链上。稳定币的第一层价值，是为非美元国家提供美元敞口；下一步则是提供美元体系中最优质、最有共识的资产，让原本接触不到的人获得配置渠道。
  • 主持人把产品路线归纳得很直接：用户以后不只持有美元，还能在波场生态买 QQQ、标普 500。孙宇晨认同，这构成转账之后的增值服务，也让波场从支付网络走向跨境资产平台。
  • 面对手续费从早年约 1 美元升至约 5—6 美元、而 Plasma 等新链主打免费转账的质疑，他承认波场确实比以前贵，但称去年已削减约 60%；持有并 staking TRX 获取能量后，用户也可以免费转账。
  • 他把转账称为“做支付宝”的第一阶段，并称波场沉淀资金已超过 1,000 亿美元。若其他链增长乏力、转账量和体量也比不上波场，他就不会把费用压到极低：用户相信品牌、网络和安全度，愿意支付溢价；RWA 做得更成功后，手续费也可能再降。

10. “老登资产”被抛弃，口碑、死亡与人生则被视为动态体验

  • 孙宇晨用“老登资产”和“新登资产”划界：白酒等老登类资产一概不看好，新登类资产则积极拥抱。这是他对时代迁移的概括表达——资本要贴近技术与新需求，而非依赖旧叙事。
  • 被问过去一年最大失败，他先回避，随后只给出“谈恋爱失败”“情感失败”。但他随即补充：它对 relationship 可能是失败，对人生却“不一定是个失败”，也可能成为一笔财富。
  • 对口碑，他坚持“还是挺重要的”，但不把舆论看作永久判决。不同人生阶段，口碑来源会变化；应当了解舆情并与之良好相处，通过交流让争议继续激荡，因为“我从来不认为观点是永恒的”。
  • 他坦言自己最缺的是对 AI 的理解与应用，终极理想也是把 AI 与现有业务结合，在新时代为个人和公司找到位置。面对死亡，他说“怕死”，也用 AI 监控身体数据；目标不是延长寿命，而是在合理寿命范围内最大化生命，并“有尊严、有体面地死去”。

11. “孙学”被定义为零成本 bootstrap，孙宇晨奖则要为 AI 时代持续迭代

  • 如果年轻人不想学“孙学”，他的第二建议是先练搏击；若要学，他称孙学“挺完美”，并说这套系统可以像 AI skill 一样“直接蒸馏、零成本安装”。目标用户是普通年轻人，而非已经含着金钥匙、能够建立自有方法的人。
  • 主持人的反对意见值得保留：孙学可能过于精益求精，并把社会推向精致利己。孙宇晨否认两者等同，称其第一步是摸清时代环境与自身条件，再选择个人利益最大化的博弈路径；它是一种博弈论，也是一种演化论，服务于从零到一的 bootstrap。
  • 他以 2016 年的主张说明“顺着时代车轮”：年轻人不要结婚、不要买房，all in 英伟达与特斯拉；他称这样做的人十年后财产会获得巨量级增长。推荐书目也延续这套思想谱系——安·兰德《源泉》、王小波《黄金时代》，以及自己的《孙学》。
  • 孙宇晨奖目前只投入财富的一小部分，因为要像打德扑一样“先看看牌”。他设想 AI 未来一天可能产生 50 个诺贝尔奖成果，奖项因此必须迭代：任何人用 AI 解题，只要通过 Lean 形式验证即可获奖；题集已有首批获奖者，但 OpenAI 尚未来领奖。

来源：X

Read on BidClub: https://bidclub.ai/e/justin-sun-deep-interview-btc-nasdaq-ai-20261016

item.title: You Know Zcash, But Railgun Lets You Use Any Asset Privately Across All Ethereum DeFi
item.description: Railgun presents itself as Ethereum’s “incognito mode,” using zero-knowledge spending to shield varied assets rather than fixed-denomination mixing; it spans five chains and has roughly $117M TVL cited on DeFiLlama. Payments—not trading—are its leading use case, but privacy sets can be weak for long-tail tokens, while broader DeFi access remains wallet-dependent and Railgun Connect is still research.
item.content:encoded:
The Edge Podcast · DeFi Dad、Nomatic、Alan · 2026-10-16 · 57 min · 原语言 EN

Railgun presents itself as Ethereum’s “incognito mode,” using zero-knowledge spending to shield varied assets rather than fixed-denomination mixing; it spans five chains and has roughly $117M TVL cited on DeFiLlama. Payments—not trading—are its leading use case, but privacy sets can be weak for long-tail tokens, while broader DeFi access remains wallet-dependent and Railgun Connect is still research.

TL;DR

  • Railgun researcher Alan pitches the protocol as “the incognito mode for Ethereum”: a suite of smart contracts creating a private address standard — the Zcash-style shielded side of Ethereum — deployed on Ethereum, Base, Arbitrum, Polygon, and BSC, with roughly $117M TVL cited on DeFiLlama. The research agenda is “how do you make it do everything that a public address can do” — tapping the EVM economy “without doxing your wallet.”
  • Nomatic distinguishes Railgun from mixers: mixers break chain of custody with fixed denominations and work poorly for “novel balances,” NFTs, and varied shitcoin portfolios, while Railgun is a lockbox inside a safe where you prove with zero knowledge that you have the right to spend. Alan says the goal is “for it to be a true wallet you can trust, with privacy, where you can put all your tokens and transact from them forever.”
  • The #1 use case is payments, not trading — consolidating 20+ wallets, paying into CEX or Hyperliquid accounts, and using payment links to private addresses — and Alan says the privacy set is very high for ETH and stablecoins but can be weak for long-tail tokens due to a cold-start problem. DeFi access depends on wallet choice (Alan says Anon has the most: Morpho, Hyperliquid, fxUSD, Beefy); Railgun Connect is research toward connecting balances to arbitrary DeFi mechanisms, not a do-it-right-now feature.
  • Alan’s hot take is that the privacy that matters is wallet-side actor blinding, while dApp-level privacy threatens DeFi’s core auditability. The target UX is a Visa terminal that just says “Approved” — “none of their business” — but black-box dApps make it harder for ordinary users to verify Aave LTVs or vault behavior, and FHE verification is “an equal trust-me-bro kind of statement... I have to trust a nerd.”
  • On the Zcash valuation disparity, Alan reframes the question around proximity to economic activity: Zcash today is “primarily for ZEC” and sits “at arm’s length” from Uniswap, CoW Swap, vaults, and stablecoins — activity he wants to participate in. He says NEAR’s tie-in has reduced that distance somewhat, but “I want my privacy mechanism to be on Ethereum”; he has used Zcash and dug out old seeds when its price moved.
  • Alan sees the Ethereum Foundation’s Kohaku work as complementary, not competitive: projects built with the Kohaku SDK are beginning to integrate Railgun contracts, and he thinks Ambire will release a Railgun-integrated wallet soon. He sees default privacy arriving as a stack, not a switch: mempool privacy and RPC privacy (he thinks the EF research is called AnonRPC) may become easier and more widespread, while Railgun remains a toggleable incognito layer. “Privacy isn’t about hiding everything”; it is about “self-selecting what you reveal to the world.”
  • RAIL’s utility is security governance: staking contracts hold “70-plus percent” of total RAIL, and stakers review upgrade proposals (such as the Base deployment) as “guardians of the Railgun ecosystem.” Transaction fees fund rewards from the treasury, distributed every two weeks; Alan thinks the year will end with just over $2M in rewards to active stakers. Alan also teased a part two on post-quantum privacy.

Digest

1. Six years of privacy slog started with a stranger reading his Etherscan

  • Alan’s origin story: trading in Telegram groups, he was asked about a position he had not shared — “you have the Collab.Land token, and you’ve talked about this trade and that trade... and that’s your wallet, right?” — and was shown his own Etherscan. His progression thesis: “you start to self-custody... and then maybe after self-custody comes privacy.”
  • The elevator pitch: Railgun is a suite of smart contracts creating a private address standard — like Zcash’s public/private split, “Railgun is handling the private side of Ethereum.” You generate a private address from your seed and use it like a 0x address; the research question is how to make it do everything a public address can, “without doxing your wallet” — “the incognito mode for Ethereum.”
  • DeFi Dad’s motivating examples: realizing he had transacted from an ENS-labeled wallet and worrying about wallet exposure through data breaches at exchanges, accounting firms, and Web2 entities.

2. Not a mixer: a lockbox in a safe, spendable by ZK proof

  • Nomatic explains that mixers aim to break chain of custody between addresses using fixed denominations — he recalls Tornado Cash denominations of 0.1, 1, 10, and 100 ETH — and says mixers work poorly for NFTs, varied shitcoin balances, or novel amounts such as 13.243 ETH. “Apples and oranges are both fruit... I believe fruit can be compared” — similar in some ways, but mechanically very different.
  • Nomatic’s analogy for Railgun is a safe with a lockbox: it can hold assets such as USDC, ETH, or DAI. Alan adds that CryptoDickbutts are another example of what someone might put in, and that mechanically “you’re doing a zero-knowledge proof that you have the right to spend from your lockbox.”
  • What Etherscan shows after shielding: a public address has put funds into Railgun; whether they went to that user’s private address or paid someone else “is left to interpretation.” From there, users can transact through CoW Swap or 0x, or use integrated wallets (Railway, Anon, Terminal, RailOxide) and WalletConnect apps such as Faceless and Token Shielder.

3. Payments are the killer app; DeFi access depends on your wallet

  • Alan’s ranking: “the number one thing that’s happening with Railgun is payments” — consolidating the 20-plus wallets many crypto users have kept separate into “one nice balance,” paying into CEX or Hyperliquid accounts (“because they want to go long XPL or something”), and using payment links to a 0zk address. The driver: people “judge you on Etherscan after you give them an address.”
  • The contracts themselves “don’t really care what other smart contracts you interact with,” but today DeFi is a curated, wallet-level experience. Alan says Anon has the most features: deposits into Morpho vaults, seeding and re-shielding Hyperliquid balances, swaps via Uniswap/0x/aggregators, minting fxUSD from shielded ETH, and Beefy farming.
  • The open research: Railgun Connect is designed to connect a Railgun balance to DeFi mechanisms. Alan says the team is working on making this seamless and that it is tricky; he imagines AI could enable an agentic experience, but calls that “a ‘soon™,’ not a do-it-right-now kind of thing.”

4. Privacy sets, ~$117M TVL, and “a state machine on a state machine”

  • Alan says privacy is “very high for a certain subset of tokens — stablecoins and ETH.” Shielding an obscure token like Artificial Inu would likely mean a weak privacy set because few people may have used it: a per-token cold-start problem. His example: $80M of ETH in Railgun could give his “peasantly $150” a strong privacy set; if a token has $300 in it and he deposits $80,000, he may be assumed to be the actor.
  • TVL is public: Nomatic cites about $117M on DeFiLlama, and Alan says Etherscan showed around $120M on Ethereum at that point, with ETH, USDC, DAI, USDT, and other tokens. Internal flows aren’t visible: if Alan sends DeFi Dad 100 ETH inside Railgun, “the only thing that you see is a state update on Ethereum.”
  • On whether Railgun is an L2: Alan says it is “basically a state machine on a state machine,” but not technically an L2. He says it has censorship-resistance and immutability properties an L2 won’t have, noting that some L2s can be shut down or have their sequencer paused.

5. The NEAR freeze: a host’s discomfort, and Alan’s line between CeFi and DeFi

  • Nomatic recalls that, during what he thinks was the Bitget hack, NEAR stopped some funds from being moved; he estimates the amount at about $49M. Alan says the capture rate was over 90%. Nomatic expresses mixed feelings: “on one hand... screw those hackers. On the other hand,” it raises concerns that a protocol can step in and act.
  • Alan’s response: “I hate a thief. I don’t like criminals, dude” — and NEAR is a centralized bridge, “you’re going through Jim Bob’s S3 bucket probably,” so he thinks intervening was the right thing to do. The error, he says, is conflating all DeFi: he does not want that kind of mechanism in DeFi, but thinks it is fine for centralized services.

6. Versus Zcash: Railgun lives where the economy is

  • Alan acknowledges the lineage: Railgun is “effectively a Zcash-style shielded mechanism for Ethereum,” borrowing concepts such as shielding. The difference: Zcash as it exists today is primarily for ZEC, while Railgun is designed for ETH, USDT, DAI, and stablecoins — because people commonly send stablecoins.
  • Nomatic asks about the price disparity, given Railgun’s usability. Alan reframes the answer as why Railgun exists: Zcash and Tornado Cash were already there in 2020, but Zcash was “at arm’s length from all the cool things that I’m doing” — Uniswap, Curve, CoW Swap, vaults, and staking. NEAR’s tie-in has reduced that distance somewhat, but Alan still wants his privacy mechanism on Ethereum.
  • Alan says he has used Zcash and, when its price started moving, dug out old seeds to see what was there. He also notes that Zcash shielded-asset research could be interesting.

7. The hot take: privacy belongs in wallets; transparency belongs in dApps

  • Alan’s framing: what matters is wallet-side “actor blinding.” Etherscan voyeurism — “oh, he uses Kraken... oh, he got this airdrop... oh, he has a Milady” — can seem cute, but is “broadly bad for the ecosystem.” The target UX is a Visa terminal: it says “Approved,” you get your coffee, and “they don’t get to judge you or say, ‘I see you’re late on your mortgage.’ They have no idea. It’s none of their business.”
  • His counter-position on dApp-level privacy: ordinary users should be able to check Aave’s loan-to-value, a vault’s payouts, or whether something is controlled by a multisig. Black-box dApps make that harder, and FHE verification “adds a certain trust element... I have to trust a nerd.” “‘Trust me, bro, I’m a mathematician’ is an equal ‘trust me, bro’ kind of statement.”
  • His regulatory analogy: imagine needing “crazy encrypted computation” to review a company’s 10-K — “the SEC would be like, ‘Nah. We’re not doing that. We’re not playing that game here.’” He is not sure DeFi should do that either, at least not yet.
  • The hosts discuss DeFi’s transparency by comparing it to a Venmo payment exposing someone’s financial history. Nomatic admits he has looked at other people’s wallets, including those of friends and investors whose success he admires, underscoring that this voyeurism is not hypothetical.

8. Kohaku, the privacy stack, and a RAIL token that’s 70% staked

  • On fears that the EF is competing with Railgun, Alan says the work is complementary. Contributors include Chainway (Turkey), which helped write Railgun’s private proof-of-innocence mechanism, and ZKNOX (France), which wrote hardware support. Alan says projects built with the Kohaku SDK are beginning to integrate Railgun contracts; he thinks Ambire will release a Railgun-integrated wallet soon.
  • Will privacy be default? Alan’s answer is “yes and no”: privacy is a stack, like browser security — the “S” in HTTP was not as ubiquitous in the period from 1994 to about 2016, followed by optional incognito mode and VPNs. He expects mempool privacy to become standard, saying he is “sick and tired of feeding Jared from Subway” through front-running and sandwiching. He also expects RPC privacy to become easier and more common; he thinks the EF research is called AnonRPC and says it can pass RPC calls over Tor. He says institutions want and need this. Railgun would remain an optional incognito layer: “privacy isn’t about hiding everything. To me, it’s more about self-selecting what you reveal to the world.”
  • RAIL mechanics: staking contracts hold “70-plus percent” of total RAIL. Stakers review upgrade proposals — most recently, whether to deploy Railgun on Base — and check that a deployment is not backdoored. Alan says treasury fees taken in basis points from transactions fund rewards every two weeks, and thinks the year will end with just over $2M in rewards to active stakers.
  • The close: Alan describes Railgun as a decentralized project seeking builders through its SDKs, including Railgun Community, Railgun Reloaded, and Kohaku, and points privacy-curious listeners to the Church of Railgun Telegram. He teases a possible part two on “the future of privacy and the whole post-quantum thing.”

来源：YouTube
